$$
{y}^{′}=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x-1}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x-1}((\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+1).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $g(x)=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields $y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x))+(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+{tan}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y({sec}^{2}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+{tan}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}({sec}^{2}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+{tan}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+{tan}^{2}⁡x.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $$
y=(-7x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((-7x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{-7x}\cdot (-7)) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(-7x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(-7x)^{x}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d684987d-da0e-5a34-884e-9b8cf8692f4f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d684987d-da0e-5a34-884e-9b8cf8692f4f" :answer-field/id #uuid "d684987d-da0e-5a34-884e-9b8cf8692f4f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-50609b1c-20c3-5c9e-b651-ed00026d39e8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-50609b1c-20c3-5c9e-b651-ed00026d39e8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-50609b1c-20c3-5c9e-b651-ed00026d39e8" :answer/id #uuid "50609b1c-20c3-5c9e-b651-ed00026d39e8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-d653dfc3-332e-578a-824c-24d06ec11b4f" :question/id #uuid "d653dfc3-332e-578a-824c-24d06ec11b4f" :question/math-academy-id "q-341944" :question/problem "Find the slope $m$ of the tangent line to the curve $y={(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=2.$

$m=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=2$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y={(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x}))+({x}^{2})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})+{x}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})-x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =xy(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =x{(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y={(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=2} & =(2){(\frac{2}{2})}^{(2)^{2}}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{2})-1) \\  & =2(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-1) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a3103677-824b-5b24-a53b-8724b60d9376"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$

We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
-2x+y=-10
$$

Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =-10 \\ (-1)\cdot (-2x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (-10) \\ 2x-y & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done!

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$

We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\frac{1}{5}x+y=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}x+y & =\frac{1}{2} \\ 10\cdot (\frac{1}{5}x+y) & =10\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) \\ 2x+10y & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done!

The standard form of the line is 

$$
2x+10y=5.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186085124 :answer-field/correct "answer-50e5beee-cd5d-5d0e-a06c-ed2bcb868f66" :answer-field/choices :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$

II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+2\ne 0.
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that, $Q({u}_{1})⊥̸Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}\ne 0.
$$

- Statement III is false since the set is not even orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7be66281-82ba-5671-8686-d76669d37ebe"] "question-4b717300-ca17-51b3-997a-8770eb9ed2a5" :question/id #uuid "4b717300-ca17-51b3-997a-8770eb9ed2a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-341490" :question/problem "$$

If $y=\operatorname{arcsch}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)],$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $x>0.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{x|\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)|}$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosecant function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\{arcsch[\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)]\} \\  & =-\frac{1}{|\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)|\sqrt{1+[\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)]^{2}}}\cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)]^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{|\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)|\sqrt{1+[\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)]^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x|\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)|}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+[\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)]^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cc44b4dd-a212-5cf1-811f-8d6f7f853e3f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-cc44b4dd-a212-5cf1-811f-8d6f7f853e3f" :answer-field/id #uuid "cc44b4dd-a212-5cf1-811f-8d6f7f853e3f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-a37e726d-bc2a-5673-bfc6-c4c9c7ba2754" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a37e726d-bc2a-5673-bfc6-c4c9c7ba2754"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a37e726d-bc2a-5673-bfc6-c4c9c7ba2754" :answer/id #uuid "a37e726d-bc2a-5673-bfc6-c4c9c7ba2754" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\ln(x))^2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-61b524cd-3bec-51a5-bff2-353476be186c" :question/id #uuid "61b524cd-3bec-51a5-bff2-353476be186c" :question/math-academy-id "q-95514" :question/problem "$$

$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

find $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
		&= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( \log_4 x + \ln x \right)\
		&= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\log_4 x) + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\ln x )\
		&= \dfrac{1}{x\ln 4} + \dfrac{1}{x}.
}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+\frac{1}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+1.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-4890c920-695d-52f8-8b20-5f7886a5c8be" :question/id #uuid "4890c920-695d-52f8-8b20-5f7886a5c8be" :question/math-academy-id "q-70887" :question/problem "Given that $y=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}$, find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The derivative of the natural logarithm is the reciprocal function:

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{4}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{4x}.\end{aligned}

"{4}^{x}\text{ }\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186314898 :question/worked-solution "To differentiate a logarithm with base $a,$ we use the formula

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{a}⁡x)=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡a}.
$$

To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}+x-3{log}_{6}⁡x) \\  & =2\cdot 3{x}^{2}+1-3\cdot \frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡6} \\  & =6{x}^{2}+1-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=3} & ={(6{x}^{2}+1-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡6})|}_{x=3} \\  & =6(3)^{2}+1-\frac{3}{3\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡6} \\  & =55-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186314045 :answer-field/correct "answer-fce43cba-9363-5793-89ef-2161d7a4191d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fce43cba-9363-5793-89ef-2161d7a4191d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fce43cba-9363-5793-89ef-2161d7a4191d" :answer/id #uuid "fce43cba-9363-5793-89ef-2161d7a4191d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "55-\frac{1}{\ln 6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ada1f0d5-c981-59b4-bce0-235ff7c6a380" :question/id #uuid "ada1f0d5-c981-59b4-bce0-235ff7c6a380" :question/math-academy-id "q-340112" :question/problem "Given the function $y=-3{log}_{2}⁡x+4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5,$ the slope of the tangent line at $x=1$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-3{log}_{2}⁡x+4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5) \\  & =-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{2}⁡x)+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-5) \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+4\cdot \frac{1}{x}+0 \\  & =-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{4}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{4}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{4}{1} \\  & =4-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a8fbe119-4292-551a-8361-7221b4390c27"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a8fbe119-4292-551a-8361-7221b4390c27" :answer-field/id #uuid "a8fbe119-4292-551a-8361-7221b4390c27" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-e7cfc336-57d9-5dec-907f-338b4a0deb28" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e7cfc336-57d9-5dec-907f-338b4a0deb28"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e7cfc336-57d9-5dec-907f-338b4a0deb28" :answer/id #uuid "e7cfc336-57d9-5dec-907f-338b4a0deb28" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4-\frac{3}{\ln 2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5fc69141-ff6d-5890-b291-b49f76733a86" :question/id #uuid "5fc69141-ff6d-5890-b291-b49f76733a86" :question/math-academy-id "q-17369" :question/problem "Given that $y=2x-5\operatorname{ln}⁡x$,  find the slope of the tangent at $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-5\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)-5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =2-5\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =2-\frac{5}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(2-\frac{5}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =2-\frac{5}{1} \\  & =2-5 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-eb26c42c-3215-5776-a674-4934970fcf28"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-eb26c42c-3215-5776-a674-4934970fcf28" :answer-field/id #uuid "eb26c42c-3215-5776-a674-4934970fcf28" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5055e728-2745-5bd6-aa2d-52f75d5a7936" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5055e728-2745-5bd6-aa2d-52f75d5a7936" "answer-73dfc5f3-9e80-528c-a5ab-77acda2a98a4" "answer-d244ce26-b20f-5f01-a9eb-9966bbe28980" "answer-85994c7d-f00b-5eeb-877e-5a8a347c02d4" "answer-564f16f8-7148-5fe5-976e-a28969e4028a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5055e728-2745-5bd6-aa2d-52f75d5a7936" :answer/id #uuid "5055e728-2745-5bd6-aa2d-52f75d5a7936" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-73dfc5f3-9e80-528c-a5ab-77acda2a98a4" :answer/id #uuid "73dfc5f3-9e80-528c-a5ab-77acda2a98a4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d244ce26-b20f-5f01-a9eb-9966bbe28980" :answer/id #uuid "d244ce26-b20f-5f01-a9eb-9966bbe28980" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85994c7d-f00b-5eeb-877e-5a8a347c02d4" :answer/id #uuid "85994c7d-f00b-5eeb-877e-5a8a347c02d4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-564f16f8-7148-5fe5-976e-a28969e4028a" :answer/id #uuid "564f16f8-7148-5fe5-976e-a28969e4028a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{9}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097817 :tutorial/content "For a general logarithm of base $a,$ the derivative is given by

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( \log_a x \right)= \dfrac{1}{x\ln a}.
$$

Also, recall that whenever $\log$ is written without a base, we can assume that it represents the base $10.$ So, we have

$$
\log x =  \log_{10} x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{log}⁡x) & =\frac{d}{dx}({log}_{10}⁡x)=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡10}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To see where this rule comes from, we can use the change-of-base formula as shown below.

$$
\log_a x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln a}
$$

Taking the derivative and using the fact that $\ln a$ is a constant, then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{a}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡a}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡a}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡a}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096894 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179722 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-18882139-e768-512f-b798-8450fe515622" "question-77ce5f28-3326-5c6e-a417-40662b67aeff"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179666 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8659922e-fb1c-5be1-95b0-fc0ad4f5b044" "question-84ef10c5-43f7-5edc-8718-6907ea19be0b" "question-2eda7c70-df6a-5426-8bab-8b4a22231bc8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-18882139-e768-512f-b798-8450fe515622" :question/id #uuid "18882139-e768-512f-b798-8450fe515622" :question/math-academy-id "q-123070" :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,5]$

- ${P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[5,7]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[1,5]$ and $[5,7]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =5-1=4, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =7-5=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=4\cdot 2=8.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-552bf9bd-d243-5f25-994a-19d9969dc968"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-552bf9bd-d243-5f25-994a-19d9969dc968" :answer-field/id #uuid "552bf9bd-d243-5f25-994a-19d9969dc968" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-92d533f1-23d6-567a-9a29-1fd69535565d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-265ebb5d-6013-56b6-a1e4-0de08d94c7d2" "answer-84f8b00f-5a24-5b47-a712-2790b187c427" "answer-912a022d-f6b3-50b7-a153-046e3669ebda" "answer-92d533f1-23d6-567a-9a29-1fd69535565d" "answer-cd801db8-41a1-5693-b151-2ece60774a80"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-265ebb5d-6013-56b6-a1e4-0de08d94c7d2" :answer/id #uuid "265ebb5d-6013-56b6-a1e4-0de08d94c7d2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-84f8b00f-5a24-5b47-a712-2790b187c427" :answer/id #uuid "84f8b00f-5a24-5b47-a712-2790b187c427" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-912a022d-f6b3-50b7-a153-046e3669ebda" :answer/id #uuid "912a022d-f6b3-50b7-a153-046e3669ebda" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92d533f1-23d6-567a-9a29-1fd69535565d" :answer/id #uuid "92d533f1-23d6-567a-9a29-1fd69535565d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cd801db8-41a1-5693-b151-2ece60774a80" :answer/id #uuid "cd801db8-41a1-5693-b151-2ece60774a80" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186275216 :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}4Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-77ce5f28-3326-5c6e-a417-40662b67aeff" :question/id #uuid "77ce5f28-3326-5c6e-a417-40662b67aeff" :question/math-academy-id "q-123067" :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,3]$

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[1,3]$ and $[3,6]$ respectively. So, we have

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[0,2]$

- ${P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,6]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186339124 :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[0,1]$

- ${P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,2]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}3Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180268 :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[2,5]$

- ${P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[0,2]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}+{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}+{y}_{j-1})Δ{y}_{j}.
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ is just the length of the interval $[2,5].$ So, we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}=5-2=3.
$$

For the sum over $j,$ we evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}+{y}_{j-1})Δ{y}_{j} & =({y}_{1}+{y}_{0})Δ{y}_{1}+({y}_{2}+{y}_{1})Δ{y}_{2}+⋯+({y}_{n}+{x}_{n-1})Δ{y}_{n} \\  & =({y}_{1}+{y}_{0})({y}_{1}-{y}_{0})+({y}_{2}+{y}_{1})({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})+⋯+({y}_{n}+{x}_{n-1})({y}_{n}-{y}_{n-1}) \\  & =({y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{0}^{2})+({y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{1}^{2})+⋯+({y}_{n}^{2}-{y}_{n-1}^{2}) \\  & =(\cancel{{y}_{1}^{2}}-{y}_{0}^{2})+(\cancel{{y}_{2}^{2}}-\cancel{{y}_{1}^{2}})+⋯+({y}_{n}^{2}-\cancel{{y}_{n-1}^{2}}) \\  & =-{y}_{0}^{2}+{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{n}^{2}-{y}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}-{0}^{2} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we finally arrive at

To demonstrate, let's look at the expression

$$
5\log_{\color{blue}4}{\color{red}7}+3\log_{\color{blue}4}{\color{red}7}.
$$

Both logarithmic terms have a base of $\color{blue}4$ and an argument of ${\color{red}7}.$ Therefore, we can combine them by adding their coefficients:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{log}_{4}⁡7+3{log}_{4}⁡7 & =(5+3){log}_{4}⁡7=8{log}_{4}⁡7\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115427 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096666 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0dd7b4b0-db82-575a-9dad-d6a7735e5596"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0dd7b4b0-db82-575a-9dad-d6a7735e5596" :question/id #uuid "0dd7b4b0-db82-575a-9dad-d6a7735e5596" :question/math-academy-id "q-114700" :question/problem "$\int [{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-1]\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{4})=\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+1].
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$

"![](images/c9/c91e196377aad64db49224cb5e38c1c8336171649708ec78b9cb80ebe6803128.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=-3{cos}^{2}⁡x+3{sin}^{2}⁡x+{x}^{2}+3,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-3{cos}^{2}⁡x+3{sin}^{2}⁡x+{x}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=-3{cos}^{2}⁡x+3{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-3{cos}^{2}⁡x+3{sin}^{2}⁡x+{x}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+{x}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+3x)\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\frac{(\pi /2)^{3}}{3}+3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}]-[-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )+\frac{(-\pi /2)^{3}}{3}+3(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =(\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{24}+\frac{3\pi }{2})-(-\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{24}-\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{12}+3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3fb31870-9443-5984-b41f-efc5c4e135b0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3fb31870-9443-5984-b41f-efc5c4e135b0" :answer-field/id #uuid "3fb31870-9443-5984-b41f-efc5c4e135b0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1b737d1d-48cd-5a7e-b7bb-f5db76229dd4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1b737d1d-48cd-5a7e-b7bb-f5db76229dd4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1b737d1d-48cd-5a7e-b7bb-f5db76229dd4" :answer/id #uuid "1b737d1d-48cd-5a7e-b7bb-f5db76229dd4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{12}+3\pi" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096667 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-85abb599-4be2-577d-9d0b-59402cc7e2bf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-85abb599-4be2-577d-9d0b-59402cc7e2bf" :question/id #uuid "85abb599-4be2-577d-9d0b-59402cc7e2bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-348918" :question/problem "![](images/28/28be65f566e93427105af6c87c46fa51f1a473363247f35a4aa481b93dc70090.png)

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2}),$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{2}$ is 

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2}6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))={sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2}).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2}6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{(x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)|}_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2} \\  & =3[(\frac{5\pi }{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{2}))-(\frac{\pi }{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))] \\  & =3[(\frac{5\pi }{2}-1)-(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)] \\  & =3(2\pi ) \\  & =6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4a8bb75e-79be-5239-bdbe-829119163778"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "c35e6115-b838-577e-80b7-a11c81db3ab4" :question/math-academy-id "q-48000" :question/problem "Calculate $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}$ for $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-3x)+3x.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-3x)$ and $h(x)=3x.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x)+h(x).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we differentiate $g(x).$ We express $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-3x)$ as the composite function

$$
g=\operatorname{ln}⁡u,\,u=4-3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-\frac{3}{u} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate $h(x)=3x:$ 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}=3
$$

Hence,

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={g}^{′}(x)+{h}^{′}(x)=-\frac{3}{4-3x}+3.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-820a30d1-df8f-5a80-a8f9-d041f414d3e8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-71483" :question/problem "Find ${y}^{′}$ for $y={log}_{2}⁡(2x+3).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{2}⁡(u),\,u=2x+3.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1e53e3f5-af7a-50b0-9c33-a1155d8c0ec1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1e53e3f5-af7a-50b0-9c33-a1155d8c0ec1" :answer-field/id #uuid "1e53e3f5-af7a-50b0-9c33-a1155d8c0ec1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-660e5a36-c7b3-5888-86e1-6b4e9b38a638" :answer-field/choices ["answer-64f2aaec-bdad-58bd-9357-db2f7aec0e9f" "answer-9a6cb00b-824e-53d9-8528-2efc1a6d7e93" "answer-660e5a36-c7b3-5888-86e1-6b4e9b38a638" "answer-8bbc0fd9-f288-5653-866a-e4f8e72943d0" "answer-abec248d-6ade-55e3-bdab-e993fd571336"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-64f2aaec-bdad-58bd-9357-db2f7aec0e9f" :answer/id #uuid "64f2aaec-bdad-58bd-9357-db2f7aec0e9f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a6cb00b-824e-53d9-8528-2efc1a6d7e93" :answer/id #uuid "9a6cb00b-824e-53d9-8528-2efc1a6d7e93" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{(2x+3)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-660e5a36-c7b3-5888-86e1-6b4e9b38a638" :answer/id #uuid "660e5a36-c7b3-5888-86e1-6b4e9b38a638" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8bbc0fd9-f288-5653-866a-e4f8e72943d0" :answer/id #uuid "8bbc0fd9-f288-5653-866a-e4f8e72943d0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{(2x+3)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-abec248d-6ade-55e3-bdab-e993fd571336" :answer/id #uuid "abec248d-6ade-55e3-bdab-e993fd571336" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{2x+3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092732 :question/problem "Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y={log}_{3}⁡(5x-2).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{3}⁡(u),\,u=5x-2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{1}{(5x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{5}{(5x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186090592 :answer-field/correct "answer-070b1605-3f0f-5052-807c-9e2da26f1b13" :answer-field/choices ["answer-845c0b40-9827-530c-894b-969a75a5872a" "answer-7e998750-c647-5300-8e4d-ccc8bad0a0cb" "answer-4f82f8a5-4d83-5410-bc3d-5d0dbb832acc" "answer-070b1605-3f0f-5052-807c-9e2da26f1b13" "answer-2d8415e7-55ff-5ae3-b4f6-b66c8c1d541d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-845c0b40-9827-530c-894b-969a75a5872a" :answer/id #uuid "845c0b40-9827-530c-894b-969a75a5872a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{(5x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7e998750-c647-5300-8e4d-ccc8bad0a0cb" :answer/id #uuid "7e998750-c647-5300-8e4d-ccc8bad0a0cb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{(5x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4f82f8a5-4d83-5410-bc3d-5d0dbb832acc" :answer/id #uuid "4f82f8a5-4d83-5410-bc3d-5d0dbb832acc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{(2x-5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-070b1605-3f0f-5052-807c-9e2da26f1b13" :answer/id #uuid "070b1605-3f0f-5052-807c-9e2da26f1b13" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{(5x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2d8415e7-55ff-5ae3-b4f6-b66c8c1d541d" :answer/id #uuid "2d8415e7-55ff-5ae3-b4f6-b66c8c1d541d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{(5x-2)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186093370 :tutorial/content "The chain rule can be used to differentiate logarithmic functions like 

$$
y = \ln (2x+1).
$$

First notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = \ln u, \qquad u = 2x+1.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}⁡u)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=2x+1,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092417 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133978 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7fb7b6f3-9396-53a9-a0b3-7b8a7a56bc38"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-7fb7b6f3-9396-53a9-a0b3-7b8a7a56bc38" :question/id #uuid "7fb7b6f3-9396-53a9-a0b3-7b8a7a56bc38" :question/math-academy-id "q-45177" :question/problem "![](images/71/71d77d6d9dda343a95b44fa60afbfee68619aa59bf9c6ba70eb229d072bf9a73.png)

:question/problem "![](images/8d/8d89477b4c1f7b976f86d1cc5d77c1729826358e1c1367e7982ccd59970c2ffd.png)

Which of the following combinations of transformations map the triangle $ABC$ to a congruent triangle?

I. A reflection in the $x$-axis, followed by a rotation of ${60}^{∘}$ counterclockwise about the point $A.$

II. A translation of $2$ units up, followed by a reflection in the line $\overset{⟷}{BC}.$

III. A rotation of ${15}^{∘}$ clockwise about a given point $B,$ followed by a translation of $3$ units up." :question/worked-solution "A rigid motion is a transformation that preserves distances. There are three types of rigid motions:

- Translations

- Rotations

- Reflections

Also, two polygons are congruent if and only if one can be mapped to another using a combination of rigid motions.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the transformations in turn.

- Combination I maps $ABC$ to a congruent triangle. Indeed, both transformations (a reflection, followed by a rotation) are rigid motions.

- Combination II maps $ABC$ to a congruent triangle. Indeed, both transformations (a translation, followed by a reflection) are rigid motions.

- Combination III maps $ABC$ to a congruent triangle. Indeed, both transformations (a rotation, followed by a translation) are rigid motions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f188ddc0-815b-5c23-abd4-3b93e5f115dc"] :db/ensure $$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\arsech x) = -\dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{1-x^2}}.

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.

$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}, &  & \,x\in (0,1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we arrive at the following basic integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (0,1) \\ \int \frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

We can now use these formulas for finding integrals. For example, let's find the integral

$$
\int \left(\dfrac{2}{3x\sqrt{1-x^2}} + \cos x \right) \textrm d x.
$$

Using the properties of integration and the formulas above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{2}{3x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{3}\int \frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168102 :tutorial/content "Recall that 
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = {\color{blue}\artanh{x}} + C, \qquad {\color{blue}x\in(-1,1)}.
$$

But we have just seen that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = {\color{red}\arcoth{x}} + C, \qquad {\color{red}x\in(-\infty,-1) \cup (1,\infty)}.
$$

Notice that the integral on the left-hand side is the same but we used different functions on the right. What is the difference, and how do we know which hyperbolic function to use?

The difference is the domain of the variable $x.$ When the $|x| < 1,$ we use the antiderivative $\artanh{x},$ otherwise we use the antiderivative $\arcoth{x}.$

For instance, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡x\,{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{artanh}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that since the limits of integration lie in the interval $(-1,1),$ we used the antiderivative $\artanh{x}.$

While, on the other hand, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x\,{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(3)-\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

</table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{(-1)}{5}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\frac{2}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cf9968b3-588b-5b53-acbc-9408f6c7a08b" "answer-field-7e75e366-3056-573c-a7c8-142b250bc11e" Suppose we have the following **singular value decomposition** (SVD) of $X{:}$ 

$$
X = U \Sigma V^T
$$

Note that in the SVD, the columns of $U$ are orthonormal, which implies that $U^T U = I$ (the identity matrix). 

Using this decomposition, the sample covariance matrix of $X$ can be derived as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T})(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}{{({U}^{T}U)}_{⏟}}_{I}Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ 

Now, notice the following:

- The matrix $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ is a diagonal $m \times m$ matrix with the eigenvalues of $C$ (in descending order) on the main diagonal.

- The matrix $V$ is an $m \times m$ matrix whose columns are the unit eigenvectors of $C.$

To summarize, if we write down the singular value decomposition of the standardized observation matrix $X,$ the columns of the matrix $V$ in the SVD are the **principal components** of the data." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193807 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a sample of $n$ observations, where each observation has $m$ features. We store this data in the $n \times m$ observation matrix $X,$ where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

![](images/fe/fe9bd930e502d38eccc99f9c9a7a4b994bfa6caed26dd0b2a2675128ef18252a.svg)

We assume the data has been mean-centered. Let $\mathbf{x}_j$ denote the $j$th column of $X.$ The sample covariance matrix, $C_X,$ is given by

![](images/12/126db3a0c2d3fde367318bab5f59bccae7dd2cab8342435e7faf7de24e690997.svg)

The **total variance** of the observed data equals the sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of $C_X$ (the trace of the matrix). That is,

$$
\textrm{Total Variance}  = \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_1] + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_2] + \cdots + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_m].
$$

How is the total variance related to the singular values of $X?$

We recall that using the singular value decomposition $X = U \Sigma V^T,$ the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_m$ of $C_X$ are related to the singular values $\sigma_1,\ldots, \sigma_m$ of $X$ by:

$$
\lambda_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} \quad \text{for } i=1,\ldots,m.
$$

 

Next, we will use this relationship to compute the total variance." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193809 :tutorial/content "To find the total variance in terms of singular values, define the change of variables $Y = XV.$ The covariance of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{Y}=\frac{1}{n-1}{Y}^{T}Y=\frac{1}{n-1}(XV)^{T}(XV)={V}^{T}{{(\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X)}_{⏟}}_{{C}_{X}}V.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $V$ contains the eigenvectors of $C_X,$ the matrix $C_Y$ is diagonal and contains the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $C_X{:}$

![](images/c3/c344eb83c1e16eba7fbb71c00ce28dc72875826b5c487a33cd2235499c94d4f3.svg)

The total variance is defined as the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the covariance matrix. A key property of the trace is that it is invariant under orthogonal transformations like $Y=XV.$ Therefore, the total variance of $Y$ is the same as the total variance of $X{:}$

$$
\textrm{Total Variance} = \text{Tr}(C_X) = \text{Tr}(C_Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i.
$$

Substituting $\lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1},$ we conclude that the total variance is *proportional to* the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{Total Variance} \:\propto\: \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma^2_i.}
$$

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193808 :tutorial/content "A nutritionist measured $3$ features among a group of clients:

- body mass index ($x_1$)

- height ($x_2$)

- weight ($x_3$)

The collected data was stored in the mean-centered observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular client. The nutritionist finds that the singular values of $X$ are 

$$
\sigma_1=12, \qquad \sigma_2=5, \qquad \sigma_3=4.
$$

The nutritionist then decides to reduce the dimensionality of the data set. To do this, they convert the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation 

$$
Y = X V_1,
$$

where $V_1$ is the $3 \times 1$ matrix containing the first principal component of the data only. As a result, $Y$ is an $n \times 1$ matrix that gives a single feature associated with each client.

What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$

The total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(12)^{2}+(5)^{2}+(4)^{2} \\  & =185.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the nutritionist used only the first principal component, the preserved variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Preserved} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(12)^{2} \\  & =144.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Preserved}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{144}{185} \\  & ≈0.778 \\  & =77.8%.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize:

- The nutritionist reduced the dimensionality of the data from $3$ (initially, each client had three features) to just $1$ (only one feature characterizes each client after the transformation).

- In doing so, $77.8\%$ of the variance is preserved in the transformed data." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192866 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100886 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-44b29d11-73a7-53f3-9fd8-f291cef7d6f9" "question-62a6fa3a-202f-5d9e-a258-2bf57d4dce4a" "question-9a20fdf0-e060-5815-bab2-1a7f6ad5204d" "question-bd264153-a0f2-5d3c-9c00-d5269ef8bbad"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100710 :question/problem "The diagram below shows the function $y=f(x).$ Plot the graph of $y=2f(x)+2.$

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =f(\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2})=f(\frac{1}{2}(x-1))\end{aligned}
$$

To plot $y=f(\frac{1}{2}(x-1)),$ we apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}x).$

![](images/ef/efac5abdc5ec66c794f01c53d14b10f51ff527699eae40d2f6d5802f7b51a15e.png)

- Then, translate it right by $1$ unit to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}(x-1)).$

{:db/id 17592186101971 :tutorial/content "Now that we're familiar with graph translations, reflections, and stretches, it's time to combine these transformations. 

We start by considering a general transformation of the form

$$
y = af\left(b(x+c)\right)+d
$$

Like the order of operations in arithmetic, the order in which transformations are applied matters. In general, the order *must* be as follows:

1\. Horizontal stretch

2\. Horizontal translation

3\. Vertical stretch

4\. Vertical translation

If that seems like a lot to take in, we have the following rule of thumb that can help us to remember the order in which to apply the transformations:

- We start by performing the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ This means we first deal with the $b(x+c)$ part. So, we *first* carry out the horizontal stretch, *followed by* the horizontal translation.

- Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ So, we *first* carry out the vertical stretch, *followed by* the vertical translation.

Finally, note that not every transformation will necessarily be present. $$
\begin{aligned}S & ={(x-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-\sqrt{2}x+\frac{1}{2}+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{2}-\sqrt{2}x.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =y+\frac{1}{2}+{y}^{2} \\  & ={y}^{2}+y+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(y)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y)=2y+1 & =0 \\ 2y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(y)=2>0.$ Therefore, $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{x})^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-1 & =0 \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{1}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{1}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{1}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-(\frac{1}{2})+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,3)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-4)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+3-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-6 & =0 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0,$ so $x=3$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=3$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(3)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}-6(3)+16} \\  & =\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}

For example, let's find the smallest distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1$ and the point $(5,1),$ shown below.

![](images/dc/dc1f5b350025a0fd0530531cfc887c148459194afe209e472701054c128f1079.png)

To solve this problem, we follow three steps:

**Step 1.** Use the distance formula to create a function $S(x,y)$ representing the *squared* distance between $(5,1)$ and a general point $P(x, y){:}$

$$
S = (x-5)^2 + (y-1)^2
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-5)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-10x+25+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+25.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Calculate the first derivative $S'(x)$ and solve $S'(x) = 0$ to find the stationary point(s).

Computing the derivative $S'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =2x-8.\end{aligned}
$$

The stationary points of $S(x)$ are the points where $S'(x) = 0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 2x-8 & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Use the first or second derivative tests to confirm that the stationary point minimizes the squared distance.

Computing the second derivative, we have

$$
S''(4) = 2.
$$

Since $S''(4) > 0,$ the point $x=4$ is a minimum of $S(x)$ by the second derivative test.

Therefore, we conclude that the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) reaches a minimum when $x = 4.$ 

Finally, since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=4$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(4)} \\  & =\sqrt{(4)^{2}-8(4)+25} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198506 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134336 :question/problem "$$
V=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\},\,B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]\}

Consider the subspace $V$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-2)\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot 5+0\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{5}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

Finally, $a=-1,$ $c=1,$ and  

$$
\frac{a}{c}=\frac{-1}{1}=-1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186132055 :answer-field/correct 17592186132060 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id - $(\textrm{T}2)$ - Translate up by $5$ units

What is a possible ordering of the appropriate transformations?" :question/worked-solution "To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the function:

$$
y=f\left(\dfrac x2-3\right)+5 = f\left(\dfrac 12(x-6)\right)+5
$$

To get $y=f\left(\dfrac 12(x-6)\right)+5,$ we could apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Apply transformation $(\textrm{T}1)\mathbin{:}$ Stretch $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=f\left(\dfrac x2 \right).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\textrm{T}3)\mathbin{:}$ Translate $y=f\left(\dfrac x2 \right)$ right by $6$ units to get the graph of 

$$
y=f\left(\dfrac12{(x-6)}\right).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\textrm{T}2)\mathbin{:}$ Translate $y=f\left(\dfrac12{(x-6)}\right)$ up by $5$ units to get the graph of 

$$
y=f\left(\dfrac12{(x-6)}\right)+5.
$$

Therefore, a possible order of transformations is

$$
(\textrm{T}1) \to (\textrm{T}3) \to (\textrm{T}2).
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-4dd5481f-091a-50a2-889d-4cab50cc426d" :question/id #uuid "4dd5481f-091a-50a2-889d-4cab50cc426d" :question/math-academy-id "q-87413" :question/problem "![](images/34/34f52b01b954b7ca3a829b43995aaf56a1def9f79b68028c55993c57b386eb30.png)

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

To plot $y=\frac{1}{2}f(\frac{1}{4}(x-1))-8,$ we apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4})}=4$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{4}x).$

- Then, translate it right by $1$ unit to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{4}(x-1)).$

- Then, stretch it by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of $y=\frac{1}{2}f(\frac{1}{4}(x-1)).$

![](images/fd/fd1ee07f396bf7561dc93cf4eb5f4098bb0c465c6f4b4a83328751d7e9a65dfa.png)

- Finally, translate it down by $8$ units to get the graph of $y=\frac{1}{2}f(\frac{1}{4}(x-1))-8.$

{:db/id "question-48d2170e-c4ab-503f-ae82-46d7eebc72a2" :question/id #uuid "48d2170e-c4ab-503f-ae82-46d7eebc72a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-87484" :question/problem "The graph of $y=2f(3x+6)+1,$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by applying **some** of the following transformations:

- $(\text{T}1)$ - Translate up by $1$ unit

- $(\text{T}2)$ - Translate left by $2$ units

- $(\text{T}3)$ - Stretch by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $y$-axis

- $(\text{T}4)$ - Stretch by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{3}$ parallel to the $x$-axis

- $(\text{T}5)$ - Stretch by a scale factor of $3$ parallel to the $x$-axis

Which of the following could be a possible ordering of the appropriate transformations?" :question/worked-solution "To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the function:

$$
y=2f(3x+6)+1=2f(3(x+2))+1
$$

To get $y=2f(3(x+2))+1,$ we could apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}4).$ Stretch $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{3}$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(3x).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}2).$ Translate $y=f(3x)$ left by $2$ units to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(3(x+2)).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}3).$ Stretch $y=f(3(x+2))$ by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=2f(3(x+2)).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}1).$ Translate $y=2f(3(x+2))$ up by $1$ unit to get the graph of 

$$
y=2f(3(x+2))+1.
$$

Therefore, a possible order of transformations is

$\,$ $(\text{T}4)\to (\text{T}2)\to (\text{T}3)\to (\text{T}1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4a61aa8e-99e2-5211-ae4e-dfb981050f40"] 2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the function:

$$
y=6f(4x-4)+5=6f(4(x-1))+5
$$

To get $y=6f(4(x-1))+5,$ we could apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}2).$ Stretch $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{4}$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(4x).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}5).$ Translate $y=f(4x)$ right by $1$ unit to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(4(x-1)).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}1).$ Stretch $y=f(4(x-1))$ by a scale factor of $6$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=6f(4(x-1)).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}3).$ Translate $y=6f(4(x-1))$ up by $5$ units to get the graph of 

$$
y=6f(4(x-1))+5.
$$

Therefore, a possible order of transformations is

The base of the logarithm is $2,$ so we use a base of $2$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡x & =5 \\ {2}^{{log}_{2}⁡x} & ={2}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $2^{\log_2 x} = x.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={2}^{5} \\ x & =32.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059695 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fa2d3b27-4298-5b73-9f1c-ae2a2ae60004" "question-9324f898-b949-55cf-ad73-91b42fed29fc"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059518 :question/problem "If $\log_7 (2x + 1) = 1,$ then what is $x?$" :question/worked-solution "To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(2x+1) & =1 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(2x+1)} & ={7}^{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $7^{\log_7 (2x + 1)} = 2x+1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+1 & =7 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059793 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6a40236b-6da0-50ec-9ab9-4d1b2b103597" "question-d546754a-f994-5144-a7ef-1e397b7589a7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059592 :question/problem "Given that $2\log_5 (x-3)+1 = 5,$ then what is the value of $x?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make $\log_5 (x-3)$ the subject of the equation by moving everything else to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{log}_{5}⁡(x-3)+1 & =5 \\ 2{log}_{5}⁡(x-3) & =4 \\ {log}_{5}⁡(x-3) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $5,$ so we use a base of $5$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡(x-3) & =2 \\ {5}^{{log}_{5}⁡(x-3)} & ={5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $5^{\log_5 (x - 3)} = x-3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & ={5}^{2} \\ x-3 & =25 \\ x & =28\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059795 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-542b7bfd-761e-58a3-80e1-933f25032116"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059594 :question/problem "If $7\log_6{x} - 3\log_6{x} = 2,$ then what is the value of  $x?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify our equation by collecting the like logarithmic terms, and isolating the logarithm, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{log}_{6}⁡x-3{log}_{6}⁡x & =2 \\ (7-3){log}_{6}⁡x & =2 \\ 4{log}_{6}⁡x & =2 \\ {log}_{6}⁡x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $9,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$

$$

Therefore,

Recall that the inverse operation of the logarithm is exponentiation. So, to isolate $x,$ we must exponentiate both sides of this equation. 

The base of the logarithm is $3,$ so we use a base of $3$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡x & =4 \\ {3}^{({log}_{3}⁡x)} & ={3}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above may look complicated, but since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $3^{(\log_3{x})}=x.$ Therefore, we get   

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={3}^{4} \\ x & =81.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x = 81$ is the solution." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059909 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175912 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76" "question-c123720e-2a57-5feb-ae6c-82695ba41c0a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76" :question/id #uuid "302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76" :question/math-academy-id "q-44539" :question/problem "Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(6,4)$ and is parallel to $3x-y=7.$" :question/worked-solution "Since parallel lines have equal slopes, the slope of the new line should be equal to the slope of the line $3x-y=7.$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-y & =7 \\ y & =3x-7\end{aligned}
$$

From the slope-intercept form, we can tell that the slope of the line is $3.$

So, we want a line with the slope $3$ that passes through the point $(6,4).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =3(x-6) \\ y-4 & =3x-18 \\ y & =3x-14\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write this equation in standard form.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-14 \\ -3x+y & =-14 \\ 3x-y & =14\end{aligned}

:db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192524 :question/problem "Let $X_1, X_2, X_3,X_4$ be I.I.D. random variables with probability density function

$$
f(x) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1,
$$

where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Find the log-likelihood function of the sample $1.3, \, 2.4, \, 1.0,\, 1.7.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent random variables with unknown parameter $\theta,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1.
$$

First, let's write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x;\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta {x}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{-(\theta +1)}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\theta +1)\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1-(\theta +1){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i} \\  & =n\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that $n=4,$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1.3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2.4+\operatorname{ln}⁡1.0+\operatorname{ln}⁡1.7≈1.67.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ≈4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\cdot 1.67 \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -1.67(\theta +1).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192798 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-33ce93bc-9b71-578c-a5f0-f916b3a30de2" "question-e67f295c-595a-59e1-89e6-05c919508212" "question-2e0fcfa7-37ec-568d-b873-d7a1d1d3286a" "question-e462cf70-9c4a-5912-9b6b-fb55715b7efa"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192522 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim \text{Exp}(\theta)$ and unknown rate parameter $\theta.$ Find the log-likelihood function of the sample $2, \, 4, \, 1, \, 3, \, 7.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n = 5$ independent exponential random variables with unknown parameter $\theta,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x, \theta) = \theta e^{-\theta x}, \qquad x \geq 0.
$$

First, let's write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta {e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =n\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =2+4+1+3+7=17\end{aligned}
$$

and $n = 5.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta \cdot 17 \\  & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -17\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192686 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a72b9dd5-5d41-5e15-9611-0fb245235173" "question-ed6e56e9-08e5-56f5-aaed-8bc6f1c64b9a" "question-f4dba462-88c8-55e1-ad6f-09af7f02eff1" "question-bf364950-64c1-5b8d-a6e8-f3296448f536" "question-5d776d5a-a6fa-564f-99d4-3a36bad98246"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192391 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{8}$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim N(\theta, 1^2),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{8},$ you're given that 

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i = 11.8, \qquad 
\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2 = 25.2.
$$

Find the log-likelihood function of the sample.

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta$ and standard deviation $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}, \qquad x \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =2.5+0.2+(-1.1) \\  & =1.6 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(2.5)^{2}+(0.2)^{2}+(-1.1)^{2} \\  & =7.5\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
