"question-7dcc2367-ae8e-5075-82b4-bcd5d8410a2a"] [17592186193806 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ be an $n \times m$ observation matrix with standardized data, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

Suppose we have the following **singular value decomposition** (SVD) of $X{:}$ 

$$
X = U \Sigma V^T
$$

Note that in the SVD, the columns of $U$ are orthonormal, which implies that $U^T U = I$ (the identity matrix). 

Using this decomposition, the sample covariance matrix of $X$ can be derived as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T})(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}{{({U}^{T}U)}_{⏟}}_{I}Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ 

Now, notice the following:

- The matrix $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ is a diagonal $m \times m$ matrix with the eigenvalues of $C$ (in descending order) on the main diagonal.

- The matrix $V$ is an $m \times m$ matrix whose columns are the unit eigenvectors of $C.$

To summarize, if we write down the singular value decomposition of the standardized observation matrix $X,$ the columns of the matrix $V$ in the SVD are the **principal components** of the data."] [17592186193807 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a sample of $n$ observations, where each observation has $m$ features. We store this data in the $n \times m$ observation matrix $X,$ where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

![](images/fe/fe9bd930e502d38eccc99f9c9a7a4b994bfa6caed26dd0b2a2675128ef18252a.svg)

We assume the data has been mean-centered. Let $\mathbf{x}_j$ denote the $j$th column of $X.$ The sample covariance matrix, $C_X,$ is given by

![](images/12/126db3a0c2d3fde367318bab5f59bccae7dd2cab8342435e7faf7de24e690997.svg)

The **total variance** of the observed data equals the sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of $C_X$ (the trace of the matrix). That is,

$$
\textrm{Total Variance}  = \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_1] + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_2] + \cdots + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_m].
$$

How is the total variance related to the singular values of $X?$

We recall that using the singular value decomposition $X = U \Sigma V^T,$ the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_m$ of $C_X$ are related to the singular values $\sigma_1,\ldots, \sigma_m$ of $X$ by:

$$
\lambda_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} \quad \text{for } i=1,\ldots,m.
$$

 

Next, we will use this relationship to compute the total variance."] [17592186193809 :tutorial/content "To find the total variance in terms of singular values, define the change of variables $Y = XV.$ The covariance of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{Y}=\frac{1}{n-1}{Y}^{T}Y=\frac{1}{n-1}(XV)^{T}(XV)={V}^{T}{{(\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X)}_{⏟}}_{{C}_{X}}V.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $V$ contains the eigenvectors of $C_X,$ the matrix $C_Y$ is diagonal and contains the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $C_X{:}$

![](images/c3/c344eb83c1e16eba7fbb71c00ce28dc72875826b5c487a33cd2235499c94d4f3.svg)

The total variance is defined as the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the covariance matrix. A key property of the trace is that it is invariant under orthogonal transformations like $Y=XV.$ Therefore, the total variance of $Y$ is the same as the total variance of $X{:}$

$$
\textrm{Total Variance} = \text{Tr}(C_X) = \text{Tr}(C_Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i.
$$

Substituting $\lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1},$ we conclude that the total variance is *proportional to* the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{Total Variance} \:\propto\: \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma^2_i.}
$$

Let's see an example."] [17592186193808 :tutorial/content "A nutritionist measured $3$ features among a group of clients:

- body mass index ($x_1$)

- height ($x_2$)

- weight ($x_3$)

The collected data was stored in the mean-centered observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular client. The nutritionist finds that the singular values of $X$ are 

$$
\sigma_1=12, \qquad \sigma_2=5, \qquad \sigma_3=4.
$$

The nutritionist then decides to reduce the dimensionality of the data set. To do this, they convert the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation 

$$
Y = X V_1,
$$

where $V_1$ is the $3 \times 1$ matrix containing the first principal component of the data only. As a result, $Y$ is an $n \times 1$ matrix that gives a single feature associated with each client.

What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$

The total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(12)^{2}+(5)^{2}+(4)^{2} \\  & =185.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the nutritionist used only the first principal component, the preserved variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Preserved} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(12)^{2} \\  & =144.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Preserved}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{144}{185} \\  & ≈0.778 \\  & =77.8%.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize:

- The nutritionist reduced the dimensionality of the data from $3$ (initially, each client had three features) to just $1$ (only one feature characterizes each client after the transformation).

- In doing so, $77.8\%$ of the variance is preserved in the transformed data."] [17592186192866 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186100710 :question/problem "The diagram below shows the function $y=f(x).$ Plot the graph of $y=2f(x)+2.$

The diagram above shows the function $y=f(x).$ Which of the following gives the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2})?$"] ["question-00f70d95-0a5c-50e2-bf6d-4e4f4b73ad51" :question/worked-solution "To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =f(\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2})=f(\frac{1}{2}(x-1))\end{aligned}
$$

To plot $y=f(\frac{1}{2}(x-1)),$ we apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}x).$

![](images/ef/efac5abdc5ec66c794f01c53d14b10f51ff527699eae40d2f6d5802f7b51a15e.png)

- Then, translate it right by $1$ unit to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}(x-1)).$

"answer-field-dc83b95f-a922-5dbb-8c6a-b520b1e028d6"] [17592186100948 :knowledge-point/questions "question-9424b3c1-d470-5046-9c40-b1dfb0dc13d1"] [17592186101971 :tutorial/content "Now that we're familiar with graph translations, reflections, and stretches, it's time to combine these transformations. 

We start by considering a general transformation of the form

$$
y = af\left(b(x+c)\right)+d
$$

Like the order of operations in arithmetic, the order in which transformations are applied matters. In general, the order *must* be as follows:

1\. Horizontal stretch

2\. Horizontal translation

3\. Vertical stretch

4\. Vertical translation

If that seems like a lot to take in, we have the following rule of thumb that can help us to remember the order in which to apply the transformations:

- We start by performing the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ This means we first deal with the $b(x+c)$ part. So, we *first* carry out the horizontal stretch, *followed by* the horizontal translation.

- Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ So, we *first* carry out the vertical stretch, *followed by* the vertical translation.

Finally, note that not every transformation will necessarily be present. In this lesson, we will consider a maximum of two graph transformations."] [17592186101093 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0] ["question-e62d164e-09b5-5d2f-b961-352e1855d4f4" :question/id #uuid "e62d164e-09b5-5d2f-b961-352e1855d4f4"] ["question-e62d164e-09b5-5d2f-b961-352e1855d4f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-344809"] ["question-e62d164e-09b5-5d2f-b961-352e1855d4f4" :question/problem "![](images/19/19ab5199ec0848b87d5ccb276e7a78ac0c7284dafb2bdeb463c15732540d43ae.png)

Let $P$ be the point on the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)$ that is closest to the point $(1,0)$ (as shown above). Find the equation defining the $x$-coordinate of the point $P.$

$\,\,2x-2\,+$

{{field-1}} $=0$"] ["question-e62d164e-09b5-5d2f-b961-352e1855d4f4" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2).$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2))^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{x})^{2} \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-1 & =0 \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{1}{2})}.
$$

$$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-bca0e45d-f143-5b0f-9307-2c5d5a1f757d" :question/worked-solution "Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,3)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-4)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+3-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-6 & =0 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0,$ so $x=3$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=3$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(3)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}-6(3)+16} \\  & =\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-bca0e45d-f143-5b0f-9307-2c5d5a1f757d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-898724a2-4a80-5adb-a3a5-35814a60b643" :answer-field/id #uuid "898724a2-4a80-5adb-a3a5-35814a60b643"] ["answer-76ef0f93-55ce-5d9f-8c84-ab1d8ac24ee0" :answer/id #uuid "76ef0f93-55ce-5d9f-8c84-ab1d8ac24ee0"] ["answer-76ef0f93-55ce-5d9f-8c84-ab1d8ac24ee0" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-76ef0f93-55ce-5d9f-8c84-ab1d8ac24ee0" :answer/value "\sqrt{7}"] ["answer-field-898724a2-4a80-5adb-a3a5-35814a60b643" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-898724a2-4a80-5adb-a3a5-35814a60b643" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-898724a2-4a80-5adb-a3a5-35814a60b643" :answer-field/correct "answer-76ef0f93-55ce-5d9f-8c84-ab1d8ac24ee0"] ["answer-field-898724a2-4a80-5adb-a3a5-35814a60b643" :answer-field/choices "answer-76ef0f93-55ce-5d9f-8c84-ab1d8ac24ee0"] ["question-bca0e45d-f143-5b0f-9307-2c5d5a1f757d" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-898724a2-4a80-5adb-a3a5-35814a60b643"] [17592186198248 :knowledge-point/questions "question-bca0e45d-f143-5b0f-9307-2c5d5a1f757d"] ["question-de1d317e-6601-5a5d-9bc7-8e4f2a0ea625" :question/id #uuid "de1d317e-6601-5a5d-9bc7-8e4f2a0ea625"] ["question-de1d317e-6601-5a5d-9bc7-8e4f2a0ea625" :question/math-academy-id "q-344847"] ["question-de1d317e-6601-5a5d-9bc7-8e4f2a0ea625" :question/problem "Find the least distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}+3$ and the point $P(2,3).$ Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}}"] ["question-de1d317e-6601-5a5d-9bc7-8e4f2a0ea625" :question/worked-solution "Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,3)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}+3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}+3-3)}^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{x}^{2}-4x+5 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{x}^{2}-4x+5 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-8x+9.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-8 & =0 \\ 4x & =8 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0.$ Therefore, $x=2$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=2$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(2)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

"question-9e2d86f5-ab99-5ef8-9f2c-0675ddcc3d5d"] [17592186199508 :tutorial/content "We can use differentiation to find the shortest distance between a point and a curve. 

For example, let's find the smallest distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1$ and the point $(5,1),$ shown below.

![](images/dc/dc1f5b350025a0fd0530531cfc887c148459194afe209e472701054c128f1079.png)

To solve this problem, we follow three steps:

**Step 1.** Use the distance formula to create a function $S(x,y)$ representing the *squared* distance between $(5,1)$ and a general point $P(x, y){:}$

$$
S = (x-5)^2 + (y-1)^2
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-5)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-10x+25+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+25.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Calculate the first derivative $S'(x)$ and solve $S'(x) = 0$ to find the stationary point(s).

Computing the derivative $S'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =2x-8.\end{aligned}
$$

The stationary points of $S(x)$ are the points where $S'(x) = 0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 2x-8 & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Use the first or second derivative tests to confirm that the stationary point minimizes the squared distance.

Computing the second derivative, we have

$$
S''(4) = 2.
$$

Since $S''(4) > 0,$ the point $x=4$ is a minimum of $S(x)$ by the second derivative test.

Therefore, we conclude that the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) reaches a minimum when $x = 4.$ 

Finally, since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=4$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(4)} \\  & =\sqrt{(4)^{2}-8(4)+25} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198506 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0] [17592186134336 :question/problem "$$

- $(\text{T}1)$ - Translate up by $1$ unit

- $(\text{T}2)$ - Translate left by $2$ units

Which of the following could be a possible ordering of the appropriate transformations?"] ["question-48d2170e-c4ab-503f-ae82-46d7eebc72a2" :question/worked-solution "To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the function:

$$
y=2f(3x+6)+1=2f(3(x+2))+1
$$

To get $y=2f(3(x+2))+1,$ we could apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}4).$ Stretch $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{3}$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(3x).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}2).$ Translate $y=f(3x)$ left by $2$ units to get the graph of 

$$
y=f(3(x+2)).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}3).$ Stretch $y=f(3(x+2))$ by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $y$-axis to get the graph of 

$$
y=2f(3(x+2)).
$$

- Apply transformation $(\text{T}1).$ Translate $y=2f(3(x+2))$ up by $1$ unit to get the graph of 

$$
y=2f(3(x+2))+1.
$$

Therefore, a possible order of transformations is

$\,$ $(\text{T}4)\to (\text{T}2)\to (\text{T}3)\to (\text{T}1).$"] ["question-48d2170e-c4ab-503f-ae82-46d7eebc72a2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["question-d546754a-f994-5144-a7ef-1e397b7589a7" :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{log}_{5}⁡(x+2) & =6 \\ {log}_{5}⁡(x+2) & =\frac{6}{3} \\ {log}_{5}⁡(x+3) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $5,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡(x+2) & =2 \\ {5}^{{log}_{5}⁡(x+2)} & ={5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${5}^{{log}_{5}⁡(x+2)}=x+2.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & ={5}^{2} \\ x+2 & =25 \\ x & =23.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d546754a-f994-5144-a7ef-1e397b7589a7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-f060ff52-77ea-5902-887f-7649c45ec084" :answer-field/id #uuid is $x?$"] ["question-542b7bfd-761e-58a3-80e1-933f25032116" :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{log}_{9}⁡x-2{log}_{9}⁡x & =1 \\ (4-2){log}_{9}⁡x & =1 \\ 2{log}_{9}⁡x & =1 \\ {log}_{9}⁡x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $9,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{9}⁡x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {9}^{{log}_{9}⁡x} & ={9}^{1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${9}^{{log}_{9}⁡x}=x.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={9}^{1/2} \\ x & =\sqrt{9} \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-542b7bfd-761e-58a3-80e1-933f25032116" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d74c0c25-3def-5bbb-a734-c7a9a9a0dc1b" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-d74c0c25-3def-5bbb-a734-c7a9a9a0dc1b"] [17592186059795 :knowledge-point/questions "question-542b7bfd-761e-58a3-80e1-933f25032116"] [17592186060906 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the equation $\log_3 x = 4.$ Can we determine $x?$

Recall that the inverse operation of the logarithm is exponentiation. So, to isolate $x,$ we must exponentiate both sides of this equation. 

The base of the logarithm is $3,$ so we use a base of $3$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡x & =4 \\ {3}^{({log}_{3}⁡x)} & ={3}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above may look complicated, but since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $3^{(\log_3{x})}=x.$ Therefore, we get   

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={3}^{4} \\ x & =81.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x = 81$ is the solution."] [17592186059909 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0] ["question-302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76" :question/id #uuid "302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76"] ["question-302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76" :question/math-academy-id "q-44539"] ["question-302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76" :question/problem "Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(6,4)$ and is parallel to $3x-y=7.$"] ["question-302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76" :question/worked-solution "Since parallel lines have equal slopes, the slope of the new line should be equal to the slope of the line $3x-y=7.$ 

To find the slope of the line $3x-y=7,$ we convert the equation to slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-y & =7 \\ y & =3x-7\end{aligned}
$$

From the slope-intercept form, we can tell that the slope of the line is $3.$

So, we want a line with the slope $3$ that passes through the point $(6,4).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =3(x-6) \\ y-4 & =3x-18 \\ y & =3x-14\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write this equation in standard form.

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-14 \\ -3x+y & =-14 \\ 3x-y & =14\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-302f16e1-b5b4-533b-be86-52df48d21b76" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-e8a593e0-a69a-5d2b-b860-de1d3f5a603d" :answer-field/id #uuid Therefore, we wish to find a line that has a slope of $-\frac{3}{4}$ and passes through the point $(0,-3).$ To find the equation of this line, we use point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-3) & =-\frac{3}{4}(x-0) \\ y+3 & =-\frac{3}{4}x \\ y & =-\frac{3}{4}x-3\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Find the log-likelihood function of the sample $1.3, \, 2.4, \, 1.0,\, 1.7.$"] [17592186192524 :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent random variables with unknown parameter $\theta,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1.
$$

First, let's write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x;\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta {x}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{-(\theta +1)}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\theta +1)\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1-(\theta +1){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i} \\  & =n\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that $n=4,$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1.3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2.4+\operatorname{ln}⁡1.0+\operatorname{ln}⁡1.7≈1.67.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ≈4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\cdot 1.67 \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -1.67(\theta +1).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186192522 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim \text{Exp}(\theta)$ and unknown rate parameter $\theta.$ Find the log-likelihood function of the sample $2, \, 4, \, 1, \, 3, \, 7.$"] [17592186192522 :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n = 5$ independent exponential random variables with unknown parameter $\theta,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x, \theta) = \theta e^{-\theta x}, \qquad x \geq 0.
$$

First, let's write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta {e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =n\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =2+4+1+3+7=17\end{aligned}
$$

and $n = 5.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta \cdot 17 \\  & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -17\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186192391 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{8}$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim N(\theta, 1^2),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{8},$ you're given that 

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i = 11.8, \qquad 
\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2 = 25.2.
$$

Find the log-likelihood function of the sample.

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta$ and standard deviation $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}, \qquad x \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$"] [17592186192391 :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=8$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta$ and variance $\sigma^2 = 1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x, \theta) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}, \qquad x \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

First, let's write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i = 11.8,$ $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2 = 25.2,$ and $n=8.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{8}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(25.2-2\theta \cdot 11.8+8{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-12.6+11.8\theta -4{\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-643be908-7887-5e6d-8262-f7b785e61769" :question/id #uuid "643be908-7887-5e6d-8262-f7b785e61769"] ["question-643be908-7887-5e6d-8262-f7b785e61769" :question/math-academy-id "q-159913"] ["question-643be908-7887-5e6d-8262-f7b785e61769" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4},{X}_{5}$ be I.I.D. random variables with probability density function

where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter. For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{10},$ you're given that

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=10$ independent random variables with unknown parameter $\theta ,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x)=\theta {x}^{-\theta -1},\,x\ge 1.
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x;\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta {x}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{-(\theta +1)}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i} \\  & =n\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}≈11.72$ and $n=10.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ≈10\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -(\theta +1)\cdot 11.72 \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -11.72(\theta +1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b≈10+11.72=21.72.
$$"] ["question-374585a1-b6ca-5c27-b592-db80b72d2e1f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c025da46-d257-5236-b4c3-eceb6426c181" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent exponential random variables with unknown parameter $\theta ,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\theta {e}^{-\theta x},\,x\ge 0.
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta {e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =n\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =3.1+6.5+4.8+7.2=21.6\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=4.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta \cdot 21.6 \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(-21.6)\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=4+(-21.6)=-17.6.
$$"] ["question-33ce93bc-9b71-578c-a5f0-f916b3a30de2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-fbb3031c-a5cc-577f-8ba0-340b2c59edc7" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=6$ independent exponential random variables with unknown parameter $\theta ,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\theta {e}^{-\theta x},\,x\ge 0.
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta {e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =n\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =4+6+9+7+2+1=29\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=6.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\theta \cdot 29 \\  & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(-29)\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=6+(-29)=-23.
$$"] ["question-2e0fcfa7-37ec-568d-b873-d7a1d1d3286a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-89791f6b-63fb-54c9-9267-5c2e7f525e4a" :answer-field/id #uuid random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. The log-likelihood function of the sample $2.5,\,0.2,\,-1.1$ is

$$
l(\theta )=-1.5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+a+b\theta +c{\theta }^{2}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =2.5+0.2+(-1.1) \\  & =1.6 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(2.5)^{2}+(0.2)^{2}+(-1.1)^{2} \\  & =7.5\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=3.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(7.5-2\theta \cdot (1.6)+3{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-1.5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-3.75)+(1.6)\theta +(-1.5){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=-3.75+(1.6)+(-1.5)=-3.65.
$$"] ["question-a72b9dd5-5d41-5e15-9611-0fb245235173" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-c198272d-0f95-5188-850b-39d8ecf53871" :answer-field/id #uuid For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{10},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}=39.4,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}^{2}=159.8.
$$

 
Given that the log-likelihood function of the sample is

$$
l(\theta )=-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+a+b\theta +c{\theta }^{2},
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and standard deviation $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$"] ["question-ed6e56e9-08e5-56f5-aaed-8bc6f1c64b9a" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=10$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}=39.4,$ ${\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}^{2}=159.8,$ and $n=10.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{10}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(159.8-2\theta \cdot 39.4+10{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-79.9)+39.4\theta +(-5){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=(-79.9)+39.4+(-5)=-45.5.
$$"] ["question-ed6e56e9-08e5-56f5-aaed-8bc6f1c64b9a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-939abb92-670e-59cb-a71d-b99cbb16a598" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =(-1.1)+0.7+(-0.5)+(-0.7)+(-1.4) \\  & =-3 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(-1.1)^{2}+(0.7)^{2}+(-0.5)^{2}+(-0.7)^{2}+(-1.4)^{2} \\  & =4.4\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=5.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(4.4-2\theta \cdot (-3)+5{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-2.5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-2.2)+(-3)\theta +(-2.5){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=-2.2+(-3)+(-2.5)=-7.7.
$$"] ["question-f4dba462-88c8-55e1-ad6f-09af7f02eff1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-4fa74bc1-cbda-547d-ad3a-17b839fe05e3" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-bf364950-64c1-5b8d-a6e8-f3296448f536"] ["question-5d776d5a-a6fa-564f-99d4-3a36bad98246" :question/id #uuid "5d776d5a-a6fa-564f-99d4-3a36bad98246"] ["question-5d776d5a-a6fa-564f-99d4-3a36bad98246" :question/math-academy-id "q-159949"] ["question-5d776d5a-a6fa-564f-99d4-3a36bad98246" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{14}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{14},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{14}{x}_{i}=26.8,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{14}{x}_{i}^{2}=264.8.
$$

Given that the log-likelihood function of the sample is

$$
l(\theta )=-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+a+b\theta +c{\theta }^{2},
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and standard deviation $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$"] ["question-5d776d5a-a6fa-564f-99d4-3a36bad98246" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=14$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{14}{x}_{i}=26.8,$ ${\sum }_{i=1}^{14}{x}_{i}^{2}=264.8,$ and $n=14.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{14}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(264.8-2\theta \cdot 26.8+14{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-132.4)+26.8\theta +(-7){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=(-132.4)+26.8+(-7)=-112.6.
$$"] ["question-5d776d5a-a6fa-564f-99d4-3a36bad98246" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-131d7498-714e-5616-b341-5ffc1f680236" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x+5) & =3 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x+5)} & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+5 & ={e}^{3} \\ 4x & ={e}^{3}-5 \\ x & =\frac{{e}^{3}-5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186110504 :question/problem "Find the exact solution to $3\ln (5x+1)-2 = 13.$"] [17592186110504 :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1)-2 & =13 \\ 3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1) & =15 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the natural logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the natural logarithm is $e,$ so we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1) & =5 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x+1)} & ={e}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $e^{\ln (5x+1)} = 5x+1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+1 & ={e}^{5} \\ 5x & ={e}^{5}-1 \\ x & =\frac{{e}^{5}-1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186110505 :question/problem "Find the values of $x$ such that $\ln(1-2x) + 5\ln(1-2x) = 4.$"] [17592186110505 :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation by collecting the like logarithmic terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x) & =4 \\ (1+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x) & =4 \\ 6\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x) & =4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x) & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the natural logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the natural logarithm is $e,$ so we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x) & =\frac{2}{3} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)} & ={e}^{2/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $e^{\ln(1-2x)} = 1-2x.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x)+3 & =9 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x) & =6 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x) & =3 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x)} & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-5x)}=1-5x.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-5x & ={e}^{3} \\ -5x & ={e}^{3}-1 \\ x & =\frac{{e}^{3}-1}{-5} \\ x & =\frac{1-{e}^{3}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-33c6eec8-2b71-56e5-96cd-913d5dc6b9ab" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d7509eb2-c256-551d-a0b2-6e744478a267" :answer-field/id #uuid \begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1 \\ (1+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1 \\ 3\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =\frac{1}{3} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} & ={e}^{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=x.$

Suppose we have the following **singular value decomposition** (SVD) of $X{:}$

$$
X = U \Sigma V^T
$$

Note that in the SVD, the columns of $U$ are orthonormal, which implies that $U^T U = I$ (the identity matrix).

Using this decomposition, the sample covariance matrix of $X$ can be derived as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C &= \frac{1}{n - 1}X^{T}X \\
&= \frac{1}{n - 1}(UΣV^{T})^{T}(UΣV^{T}) \\
&= \frac{1}{n - 1}(VΣ^{T}U^{T})(UΣV^{T}) \\
&= \frac{1}{n - 1}VΣ^{T}(U^{T}U)_(⏟)_(I)ΣV^{T} \\
&= V(\frac{1}{n - 1}Σ^{T}Σ)V^{T}
\end{aligned}
$$

The expression

$$
\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma
$$

represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C$.

Now, notice the following:

- The matrix $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ is a diagonal $m \times m$ matrix with the eigenvalues of $C$ (in descending order) on the main diagonal.
- The matrix $V$ is an $m \times m$ matrix whose columns are the unit eigenvectors of $C$.

To summarize, if we write down the singular value decomposition of the standardized observation matrix $X$, the columns of the matrix $V$ in the SVD are the **principal components** of the data."] [17592186193807 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a sample of $n$ observations, where each observation has $m$ features. We store this data in the $n \times m$ observation matrix $X$, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x_{11} & x_{12} & … & x_{1m} \\ x_{21} & x_{22} & … & x_{2m} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ x_{n1} & x_{n2} & … & x_{nm}\end{bmatrix}
$$

We assume the data has been mean-centered. Let $\mathbf{x}_j$ denote the $j$th column of $X$. The sample covariance matrix, $C_X$, is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}Var[x_{1}] & … & Cov[x_{1}, x_{m}] \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ Cov[x_{m}, x_{1}] & … & Var[x_{m}]\end{bmatrix}
$$

The **total variance** of the observed data equals the sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of $C_X$ (the trace of the matrix). That is,

$$
\textrm{Total Variance} = \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_1] + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_2] + \cdots + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_m]
$$

How is the total variance related to the singular values of $X$?

We recall that using the singular value decomposition

$$
X = U \Sigma V^T
$$

the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_m$ of $C_X$ are related to the singular values $\sigma_1,\ldots, \sigma_m$ of $X$ by:

$$
\lambda_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} \quad \text{for} i=1,\ldots,m
$$

Next, we will use this relationship to compute the total variance."] [17592186193809 :tutorial/content "To find the total variance in terms of singular values, define the change of variables $Y = XV$. The covariance of $Y$ is given by

$$
C_{Y} = \frac{1}{n - 1}Y^{T}Y = \frac{1}{n - 1}(XV)^{T}(XV) = V^{T}(\frac{1}{n - 1}X^{T}X)_(⏟)_(C_{X})V
$$

Since $V$ contains the eigenvectors of $C_X$, the matrix $C_Y$ is diagonal and contains the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $C_X{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}λ_{1} & … & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & … & λ_{m}\end{bmatrix}
$$

The total variance is defined as the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the covariance matrix. A key property of the trace is that it is invariant under orthogonal transformations like $Y=XV$. Therefore, the total variance of $Y$ is the same as the total variance of $X{:}$

$$
\textrm{Total Variance} = \text{Tr}(C_X) = \text{Tr}(C_Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i
$$

Substituting

$$
\lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}
$$

we conclude that the total variance is *proportional to* the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{Total Variance} \:\propto\: \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma^2_i.}
$$

$$

The nutritionist then decides to reduce the dimensionality of the data set. To do this, they convert the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation

$$

$$

where $V_1$ is the $3 \times 1$ matrix containing the first principal component of the data only. As a result, $Y$ is an $n \times 1$ matrix that gives a single feature associated with each client.

What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X$?

![](images/b2/b2867f8f918683d9c66378b2beb87984a95924206e8830c7232a2802815d6737.png)"] [17592186101971 :tutorial/content "Now that we're familiar with graph translations, reflections, and stretches, it's time to combine these transformations.

What is the missing expression?"] [17592186199508 :tutorial/content "We can use differentiation to find the shortest distance between a point and a curve.

To solve this problem, we follow three steps:

**Step 1.** Use the distance formula to create a function $S(x,y)$ representing the *squared* distance between $(5,1)$ and a general point $P(x, y){:}$

$$
S = (x-5)^2 + (y-1)^2
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-5)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-10x+25+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+25.\end{aligned}

Computing the derivative $S'(x),$ we get

$$

$$

The stationary points of $S(x)$ are the points where $S'(x) = 0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$

$$

$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y={x}^{2x+1}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2x+1}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(2x+1)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+(2x+1)\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2x+1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\frac{2x+1}{x}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={x}^{2x+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2x+1}(\frac{2x+1}{x}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{2x+1}(\frac{2x+1}{x}+\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2x}\cdot x(\frac{2x+1}{x}+\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2x}(2x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=2x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1.$"} {:db/id 17592186504618 :question/id #uuid "358ad886-8781-5867-add0-1dfbbd99e7fd" :question/math-academy-id "q-138791"} {:db/id 17592186504623 $$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{2x+3}\cdot 2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+\frac{2x}{2x+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+\frac{2x}{2x+3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(2x+3)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\,(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x))+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x)) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\cdot \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2x+1}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\,(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=0} & ={(\sqrt{2(0)+1})}^{(0)^{2}+1}(0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2(0)+1)+\frac{(0)^{2}+1}{2(0)+1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(2x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x))+(2x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+2x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+2x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2(\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$"} {:db/id 17592186504637 :question/id #uuid "650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db" :question/math-academy-id "q-341951"} {:db/id 17592186504656 :question/id #uuid "965ab36a-7265-52be-bed3-0fcb25681407" :question/math-academy-id "q-341907"} {:db/id 17592186504663 :question/id #uuid "a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/math-academy-id "q-138863"} {:db/id 17592186048919} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f14cc015-61de-559e-9d6e-4f7e934ed9c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln(2x)+1" :db/id 17592186494890}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f14cc015-61de-559e-9d6e-4f7e934ed9c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln(2x)+1" :db/id 17592186494890} :answer-field/id #uuid "a47a029c-812d-5ac8-b753-06da557530dc" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186494995} {:answer/id #uuid "f14cc015-61de-559e-9d6e-4f7e934ed9c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\ln(2x)+1" :db/id 17592186494890} {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} {:activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186065202} :activity/id #uuid "2c535ceb-c030-5aed-b263-486be04ce20c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048773 :topic/id #uuid "bd7555e9-f98c-551c-968c-84222eeed14d" :topic/math-academy-id 294} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065202 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065395 :tutorial/content "**Logarithmic differentiation** is a technique to compute derivatives that are difficult to find using the usual rules of differentiation, such as the product, quotient, and chain rules.

Let's consider the following function.

$$
y = x^x
$$

We aim to compute $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$ However, in this case, we note the following:

- Both the base and the exponent are functions of $x.$

- This means we cannot apply the power rule since the exponent is not a fixed number.

- We also cannot apply the rules for differentiating exponentials since the base is not a fixed number.

So instead, we'll use logarithmic differentiation. We proceed as follows:

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $x$ using implicit differentiation and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Now, we solve for $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  y\left( \ln x + 1 \right).
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y=x^x{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = x^x \left( \ln x + 1 \right)
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "21321352-0483-513c-828f-f1c46306015a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6087 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\cdot \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2x+1}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\,(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}$ at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=0} & ={(\sqrt{2(0)+1})}^{(0)^{2}+1}(0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2(0)+1)+\frac{(0)^{2}+1}{2(0)+1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

We have the function 

$$
y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\cdot \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2x+1}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\,(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}$ at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=0} & ={(\sqrt{2(0)+1})}^{(0)^{2}+1}(0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2(0)+1)+\frac{(0)^{2}+1}{2(0)+1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

$$
y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(2x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x))+(2x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+2x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+2x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2(\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{2x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨3(0)+5,1-{0}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨5,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+5),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨3,-3(0)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨5,1⟩+u⟨3,0⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186400247 :question/id #uuid "1276b48a-33df-5447-9033-1c8e5ee23a8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-126841"} {:db/id 17592186405125 :question/id #uuid "33bfb8ae-51e5-575a-aee2-202f3434e957" :question/math-academy-id "q-32876" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "109c8716-781f-5d87-93da-32c8a82a52af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i-\frac{3}{2}\,k+u(\pi \,i+\,k)" :db/id 17592186405127} {:answer/id #uuid "2a440298-d0fd-5f7c-ade9-88076046ff22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u(\pi \,i+\,j)" :db/id 17592186405128} {:answer/id #uuid "62d667da-2ed7-5305-afe2-d228189c5402" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u(\pi \,j+\,k)" :db/id 17592186405129} {:answer/id #uuid "6b671d99-5618-53cb-8be2-7e346528c73a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u(-\pi \,j-\,k)" :db/id 17592186405130} {:answer/id #uuid "e549fd1f-32f0-5d47-bc19-3d8ea851a377" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u(i+\pi \,j+\,k)" :db/id 17592186405131}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186405129} :answer-field/id #uuid "cc1f347e-fe06-5ef7-a082-5d1425a121dd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186405126}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k$ at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2}),$ parametrized for real values of $u$ so that increasing $u$ follows the direction of increasing $t$?" :question/worked-solution "The point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t &=-1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t &=0 \\ t &=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{3}{2}).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{3}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{3}{2}) & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,j+\,k \\  & =0\,i+\pi \,j+\,k \\  & =\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is

$$
R(u)=-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u\,(\pi \,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186433175 :question/id #uuid "f8d1a00d-2251-5725-a02b-3b2319318fd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-126832"} {:db/id 17592186119945 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2{t}^{2}-t,5-3{t}^{2}⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨-1,2⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-3{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨4t-1,-6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨-1\,,\,2⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨-1,2⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨-1,2⟩ \\ ⟨4t-1,-6t⟩ & =c⟨-1,2⟩ \\ ⟨4t-1,-6t⟩ & =⟨-c,2c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4t-1 &=-c \\ -6t &=2c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=-4t+1.$ Substituting $c=-4t+1$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6t & =2(-4t+1) \\ -6t & =-8t+2 \\ 2t & =2 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨-1,2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2(1)^{2}-1,5-3(1)^{2}⟩=⟨1,2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨-1,2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186120216 :question/id #uuid "5e918f3b-d930-5ea5-9b21-8651bb576465" :question/math-academy-id "q-32918"
