"Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2{t}^{2}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,2{e}^{t}⟩$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel." :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨4t,\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ & =c\,⟨4t,\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ & =⟨4ct,\,c{e}^{t},\,2c{e}^{t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2} &=4ct \\ {e}^{t} &=c{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t} &=2c{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second and third equations, we obtain that $c=1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2} & =1\cdot 4t \\ {t}^{2} & =2t \\ {t}^{2}-2t & =0 \\ t(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=0$ and $2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨2(0)^{2},\,{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩ \\ r(2) & =⟨2(2)^{2},\,{e}^{2},\,2{e}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,{e}^{2},\,2{e}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(0,1,2)$ and $(8,{e}^{2},2{e}^{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186262664 :question/id #uuid "15bef614-c58b-5a73-8f54-ec8a2bc3ef51" :question/math-academy-id "q-126901" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03f4eddd-9c61-5352-a69a-1571210da725" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-5,-1)$ and $(\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27})$" :db/id 17592186259911} {:answer/id #uuid "11fe2bb9-1108-5d28-b12c-8890cff2d165" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{4}{3},\frac{5}{9})$  and $(0,0)$" :db/id 17592186260032} {:answer/id #uuid "5e5624d4-89b1-542b-b638-adfb8d2a014e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-5,-1)$ and $(0,0)$" :db/id 17592186260684} {:answer/id #uuid "fa38c570-2ffe-5805-b302-902cb4c665be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,0)$ and $(\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27})$" :db/id 17592186262061} {:answer/id #uuid "fd77e1df-98bd-5a78-a540-748adbdc49c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(3,1)$ and $(\frac{4}{3},\frac{5}{9})$" :db/id 17592186262096}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186259911} :answer-field/id #uuid "7308447e-ddce-597a-891f-38f71ec1133a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262317}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨4t-{t}^{2},{t}^{3}⟩,$ find all points at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨2,1⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨2,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =⟨2c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4-2t &=2c \\ 3{t}^{2} &=c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2-t.$ Substituting in the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2} & =2-t \\ 3{t}^{2}+t-2 & =0 \\ (3t-2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=-1,\frac{2}{3}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨4(-1)-(-1)^{2},(-1)^{3}⟩=⟨-5,-1⟩ \\ r(\frac{2}{3}) & =⟨4(\frac{2}{3})-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2},{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}⟩=⟨\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-5,-1)$ and $(\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}).$"} {:db/id 17592186284532 :question/id #uuid "5a127c57-e392-5180-8b85-86041bead0c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-165038" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "580c3843-6361-5a93-8e93-aa4eecc3f021" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(24,26)" :db/id 17592186282438} {:answer/id #uuid "95ec2ae6-b848-5b2c-9e73-71480e6476c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-9,-4)" :db/id 17592186282983} {:answer/id #uuid "9978da76-99f6-51aa-835d-d6470ba9b397" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-7,-4)" :db/id 17592186283023} {:answer/id #uuid "c39a49da-d2c5-5e18-8270-20d823e49792" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-9,-4)$ and $(-8,-6)$" :db/id 17592186283395} {:answer/id #uuid "ca04d778-71e9-52fd-ba77-a58b5aaf9a03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-7,-4)$ and $(24,26)$" :db/id 17592186283453}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282438} :answer-field/id #uuid "543918ac-60ea-556f-87e9-9fe723e51c77" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284072}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{5}-8,2{t}^{4}-6⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty )$, find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{5}-8),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{4}-6)⟩ \\  & =⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ ⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩ & =c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ ⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩ & =⟨c,\frac{4c}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}5{t}^{4} &=c \\ 8{t}^{3} &=\frac{4c}{5}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=5{t}^{4}.$ Substituting $c=5{t}^{4}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{t}^{3} & =\frac{4(5{t}^{4})}{5} \\ 8{t}^{3}-4{t}^{4} & =0 \\ 4{t}^{3}(2-t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=2.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨(2)^{5}-8,2(2)^{4}-6⟩=⟨24,26⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(24,26).$"} {:db/id 17592186284533 :question/id #uuid "41750cbe-5e6f-57d4-bbba-88d4814fe1e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-165040"} {:db/id 17592186284534 :question/id #uuid "001e493a-c5af-5f11-9758-cd2ce7d048b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-165041"} {:db/id 17592186284535 :question/id #uuid "c1d5d096-073b-5c49-80fa-a124c3af6414" :question/math-academy-id "q-165042" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05b526ee-e645-545d-9d38-eba3bf488f13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(e,\frac{5}{4})$ and $({e}^{-2},\frac{1}{2})$" :db/id 17592186281738} {:answer/id #uuid "14e0f6aa-69fa-5a2a-a5a2-05425a8ac3c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\frac{1}{2})" :db/id 17592186281883} {:answer/id #uuid "5c2c1ef9-8c20-5ce3-95b9-c866ecb62eb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "({e}^{2},\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186282469} {:answer/id #uuid "944b8abb-39ab-55bb-808e-d4b88ed9adfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,\frac{1}{2})$ and $({e}^{2},\frac{5}{2})$" :db/id 17592186282963} {:answer/id #uuid "bb28ac5d-2a0c-5e78-8e08-1b94f7e7ed42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(e,\frac{5}{4})" :db/id 17592186283305}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186281883} :answer-field/id #uuid "f0b7424d-a230-5a57-a288-0f3d6f9aa64c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284358}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)={e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel." :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} &=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} &=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186284536 :question/id #uuid "fc3f1136-302e-5c6a-a6a1-4ab2d796baa7" :question/math-academy-id $$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t-1})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨{t}^{3}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,{e}^{t-1}⟩ & =c\,⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{t}^{3} &=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ {e}^{t} &=c{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t-1} &=c{e}^{t-1}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second and third equations, we obtain that $c=1.$ Substituting $c=1$ into the first equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2}(t-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=0$, and $t=3.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{3},\,{e}^{0},\,{e}^{0-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,{e}^{-1}⟩ \\ r(3) & =⟨{3}^{3},\,{e}^{3},\,{e}^{3-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨27,\,{e}^{3},\,{e}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(0,1,{e}^{-1})$ and $(27,{e}^{3},{e}^{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186363527 :question/id #uuid "193b3ef5-bb74-515e-aa2f-4427c5bb5f15" :question/math-academy-id "q-165044"} {:db/id 17592186398604 :question/id #uuid "29b73a1c-11c1-5790-9fa9-ce94ade43d27" :question/math-academy-id "q-165039"} {:db/id 17592186410824 :question/id #uuid "eb19afc5-d677-5f22-bac0-92428e650b61" :question/math-academy-id "q-126900" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "38f7dbd3-9ac6-59ba-822d-baee2e1a48d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3,-5)" :db/id 17592186410818} {:answer/id #uuid "4ad7606a-78cf-5b5a-aad3-516d0783136b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,3)" :db/id 17592186410819} {:answer/id #uuid "6e2a15f9-1731-51c6-a7aa-e028d3d2c84e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,7)" :db/id 17592186410820} {:answer/id #uuid "b2e66482-ad5e-56f0-ab9c-0187ad900545" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,-1)" :db/id 17592186410821} {:answer/id #uuid "c15d36f2-d954-5b67-a997-5ab2ddb7afaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(8,-9)" :db/id 17592186410822}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410818} :answer-field/id #uuid "236f2410-bb87-524a-b10a-c030da587949" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410823}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-2t,4t-1⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨-1,1⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨-1\,,\,1⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨-1,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨-1,1⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,4⟩ & =c⟨-1,1⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,4⟩ & =⟨-c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2t-2 &=-c \\ 4 &=c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we obtain that $c=4.$ Substituting $c=4$ into the first equation, we get $t=-1.$ 

Therefore, $⟨-1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{2}-2(-1),4(-1)-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-5⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨-1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(3,-5).$"} {:db/id 17592186503676 :question/id #uuid "3a122c89-2594-51a0-a191-07ea14a78a1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-32893"} $$

$$

$r(t)$ are perpendicular." :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j]\cdot (i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1-\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{1}{{t}^{2}} & =0 \\ t-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}} & =0 \\ {t}^{4} & =1 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=\pm 1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1)=1\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j=\,i+j, \\ r(-1)=(-1)\,i+\frac{1}{(-1)}\,j=-\,i-j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1).$"} {:db/id 17592186345103 :question/id #uuid "4ed3b4a4-4334-5910-b956-ca1595cafddd" :topic/math-academy-id 1792} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120913 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121135 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve $C$ parametrized by the vector-valued function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \langle t+1, \: t^2 +1\rangle, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

Differentiating this function, we get

$$
\mathbf f'(t) = \langle 1, \: 2t\rangle.
$$

Evaluating this function and its derivative at $t=0,$ we get the following pair of vectors:

$$
\mathbf f(0)  =  \left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle, \qquad \mathbf f'(0)  =  \left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle
$$

If we view $\mathbf{f}'(0)$ as a vector attached to the tip of the position vector $\mathbf f(0),$ then it will be tangent to the curve $C,$ as shown below.

![](images/85/854d16c788836f784d739f73063354fa3ca2ad233f03cce53b99e5764449f585.png)

Since $\mathbf f'(0) \neq \mathbf{0},$ it serves as a direction vector for the tangent line to the curve at $\mathbf f(0).$ The equation of this line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(u) & =f(0)+u{f}^{′}(0) \\  & =⟨1,1⟩+u⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1+u,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $u \in (-\infty, \infty).$

In general, if a curve $C$ is parametrized by a vector function $\mathbf f(t),$ then the vector $\mathbf f'(t)$ gives a **tangent vector** to $C$ at $\mathbf{f} (t),$ provided that $\mathbf f'(t)\neq \mathbf{0}.$

For a fixed $t$ in the domain of $\mathbf{f}(t),$ the equation of the corresponding tangent line is

$$
\mathbf{R}(u) = \mathbf{f}(t) + u\mathbf{f}'(t), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

Furthermore, the vector $\mathbf f'(t)$ always points in the direction that the curve $C$ is oriented. In our example above, as $t$ increases and passes through the point $(1,1),$ the curve is transversed from left to right, and the direction of the vector $\mathbf{f}'(0)$ is also from left to right." $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-2t,4t-1⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨-1,1⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨-1\,,\,1⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨-1,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨-1,1⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,4⟩ & =c⟨-1,1⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,4⟩ & =⟨-c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2t-2 &=-c \\ 4 &=c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we obtain that $c=4.$ Substituting $c=4$ into the first equation, we get $t=-1.$ 

Therefore, $⟨-1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$

$$

$$

$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨-1\,,\,2⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨-1,2⟩.$ So, we have

$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4t-1 &=-c \\ -6t &=2c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=-4t+1.$ Substituting $c=-4t+1$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6t & =2(-4t+1) \\ -6t & =-8t+2 \\ 2t & =2 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨-1,2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}5{t}^{4} &=c \\ 8{t}^{3} &=\frac{4c}{5}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}8{t}^{3} & =\frac{4(5{t}^{4})}{5} \\ 8{t}^{3}-4{t}^{4} & =0 \\ 4{t}^{3}(2-t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨(2)^{5}-8,2(2)^{4}-6⟩=⟨24,26⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t &=-1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t &=0 \\ t &=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,j+\,k\end{aligned}

$$

$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨2,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =⟨2c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4-2t &=2c \\ 3{t}^{2} &=c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2-t.$ Substituting in the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2} & =2-t \\ 3{t}^{2}+t-2 & =0 \\ (3t-2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=-1,\frac{2}{3}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨4(-1)-(-1)^{2},(-1)^{3}⟩=⟨-5,-1⟩ \\ r(\frac{2}{3}) & =⟨4(\frac{2}{3})-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2},{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}⟩=⟨\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-5,-1)$ and $(\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}).$"} :step/id #uuid "9a79291f-1a57-5bc2-94db-68fc1780e073" :step/next {:db/id :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} &=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} &=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$"} :step/id #uuid "feabdf5c-4763-5d3a-872a-568b04e425bd"} {:db/id 17592186510527 :step/content {:db/id 17592186345102 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "70c234f6-092e-5f46-865a-425945404213" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-1,0)$ and $(1,0)$" :db/id 17592186343206} {:answer/id #uuid "72377fdc-c5c4-5cad-be35-e357b4b262ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$" :db/id 17592186343227} {:answer/id #uuid "8be39f08-c60d-56cb-867b-ae591af34e37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,-1)" :db/id 17592186343461} {:answer/id #uuid "9f960098-4e3f-597c-a84f-8d0dfb1daa4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,0)" :db/id 17592186343646} {:answer/id #uuid "ee8ce6f6-003a-5a0f-82e6-f33b9254bcdd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,1)" :db/id 17592186344335}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343227} :answer-field/id #uuid "c1ca2441-2869-5b83-a4db-5247f47eb190" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344834}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2a9495b4-c709-53eb-875a-846142be09cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-75521" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular." :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
3x-4y=-3.
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done!

Then, we will simplify it into standard form.

To construct the point-slope form of the line, we need a point and a slope. We already have two points, so we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{7-0}{4-0}=\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use this slope along with one of the points to write the point-slope form equation of the line. It doesn't matter which point we choose, but let's choose $(0,0).$ The point-slope equation is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =\frac{7}{4}(x-0) \\ y & =\frac{7}{4}x\end{aligned}
$$

To simplify the point-slope formula into standard form, we first multiply by $4$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{7}{4}(x) \\ 4\cdot (y) & =4\cdot \frac{7}{4}(x) \\ 4y & =7x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we move the variables to the left side and the constant to the right side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4y & =7x \\ -7x+4y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply by $-1$ to make the $x$-coefficient positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}-7x+4y & =0 \\ (-1)\cdot (-7x+4y) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 7x-4y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the standard form of the equation is $7x-4y=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186501213 :question/id #uuid "b34b9e0f-ca1a-53ee-8948-5e07722771b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72425" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aa1d2cc4-2934-5c01-acf3-e4688de64dff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x-y=6" :db/id 17592186500819} {:answer/id #uuid "c0d0840e-b8f1-5833-899d-775ab6668a32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y=3" :db/id 17592186500867} {:answer/id #uuid "c3d3f7b4-e921-553d-88ad-be60876e12b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=2x-3" :db/id 17592186500877} {:answer/id #uuid "ca9d0db1-1d42-546b-8c61-bc0bc89d225c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4x+y=-6" :db/id 17592186500896} {:answer/id #uuid "cf99202c-1f33-5c86-9aa3-ff042e4be5ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y=4" :db/id 17592186500913}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186500819} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ee1d5f3-79b0-529f-9d27-584c54dd513d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501034}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "What is the equation of the line that passes through the points $(1,-2)$ and $(3,6)$, expressed in standard form?" :question/worked-solution "First, we will construct the point-slope form of the line. Then, we will simplify it into standard form.

To construct the point-slope form of the line, we need a point and a slope. We already have two points, so we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{6-(-2)}{3-1}=\frac{8}{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use this slope along with one of the points to write the point-slope form equation of the line. It doesn't matter which point we choose, but let's choose $(1,-2).$ The point-slope equation is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =4(x-1) \\ y+2 & =4(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we simplify the point-slope formula into standard form, moving the variables to the left side and the constant to the right side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2 & =4(x-1) \\ y+2 & =4x-4 \\ y & =4x-6 \\ -4x+y & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply by $-1$ to make the $x$-coefficient positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x+y & =-6 \\ (-1)\cdot (-4x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (-6) \\ 4x-y & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the standard form of the equation is $4x-y=6.$"} {:db/id 17592186048936} {:db/id 17592186049169} {:db/id 17592186049201} {:db/id 17592186049869} {:db/id 17592186050320} {:answer-field/id #uuid "ca145851-e9d5-53d0-b524-37f7de7eeb0b" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186085124} {:answer-field/id #uuid "6f29fa38-38be-5d7a-8b04-017c959f4e64" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186085125} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e3b16fa4-d46b-583d-a0b9-6bff52c9a949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2x + y = 10" :db/id 17592186086455} {:answer/id #uuid "1bcdf890-3781-5cd5-80f0-19c9f1cc70b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "y = 2x - $$
ax+by=c,
$$

where

- $a,b,$ and $c$ are all integers,

- $a \geq 0,$ and

- $a,b,$ and $c$ have no common factors.

Note that we always write $x$ *before* $y$ on the left-hand side!

Let's see some examples:

- The equation $2x - y= -5$ is in standard form. Indeed, the variables are on the left-hand side, while the constant term is on the right-hand side:

$$
\underbrace{2x - y}_{\textrm{variables}} \quad = \underbrace{-5\phantom{y}}_{\textrm{constant}}
$$

 
All coefficients are integers (namely, $2,$ $-1,$ and $-5$) and don't have common factors greater than $1.$ Also, the coefficient of $x$ is non-negative ($2$).

- The equation $-3x + y = 1$ is *not* in standard form because the coefficient of $x$ is negative ($-3$).

- The equation $2x+4y = -10$ is *not* in standard form because the coefficients $(2,4,$ and $-10)$ have a common factor of $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x-1 \\ y-2x & =-1 \\ -2x+y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now the equation is in the form $ax+by=c.$ However, it violates the rule $a \geq 0.$ We can fix this by multiplying the equation by $-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =-1 \\ (-1)\cdot (-2x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (-1) \\ 2x-y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a \geq 0.$ So, we are done!

To construct the point-slope form of the line, we need a point and a slope. We already have two points, so we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{7-0}{4-0}=\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use this slope along with one of the points to write the point-slope form equation of the line. It doesn't matter which point we choose, but let's choose $(0,0).$ The point-slope equation is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =\frac{7}{4}(x-0) \\ y & =\frac{7}{4}x\end{aligned}
$$

To simplify the point-slope formula into standard form, we first multiply by $4$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{7}{4}(x) \\ 4\cdot (y) & =4\cdot \frac{7}{4}(x) \\ 4y & =7x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we move the variables to the left side and the constant to the right side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4y & =7x \\ -7x+4y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply by $-1$ to make the $x$-coefficient positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}-7x+4y & =0 \\ (-1)\cdot (-7x+4y) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 7x-4y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the standard form of the equation is $7x-4y=0.$"} :step/id #uuid "b7421da9-e8bc-5823-9858-330f84d2ecf1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186501292}} {:db/id 17592186501292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186501213 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aa1d2cc4-2934-5c01-acf3-e4688de64dff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x-y=6" :db/id 17592186500819} {:answer/id #uuid "c0d0840e-b8f1-5833-899d-775ab6668a32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y=3" :db/id 17592186500867} {:answer/id #uuid "c3d3f7b4-e921-553d-88ad-be60876e12b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=2x-3" :db/id 17592186500877} {:answer/id #uuid "ca9d0db1-1d42-546b-8c61-bc0bc89d225c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4x+y=-6" :db/id 17592186500896} {:answer/id #uuid "cf99202c-1f33-5c86-9aa3-ff042e4be5ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y=4" :db/id 17592186500913}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186500819} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ee1d5f3-79b0-529f-9d27-584c54dd513d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501034}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b34b9e0f-ca1a-53ee-8948-5e07722771b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72425" :question/problem "What is the equation of the line that passes through the points $(1,-2)$ and $(3,6)$, expressed in standard form?" :question/worked-solution "First, we will construct the point-slope form of the line. Find $‖Q(x)‖$, where $x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ \sqrt{5}\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q(x)‖ & =‖x‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198979 :question/id #uuid "063b2ff3-4387-5a0a-88b2-8a1c68641ed4" :question/math-academy-id "q-40516" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198448 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "455b3713-34a3-535d-8baf-d279a0341e9f" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Angle Preserving Property of Orthogonal Linear Transformations"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29e1aa1e-de86-5141-a747-49b7df88362b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186324305} {:answer/id #uuid "2bb428da-53ea-533b-ad36-0e999294e68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186324318} {:answer/id #uuid "2ee62035-a9e5-5f7f-9961-5d46b2a9cb27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186324345} {:answer/id #uuid "3f1e464f-a9e3-5cb7-9c86-438e31176d92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186324478} {:answer/id #uuid "abecbcfc-c2c9-55b7-a6bd-b251b89a9b98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186325432}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "3f1e464f-a9e3-5cb7-9c86-438e31176d92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186324478} :answer-field/id #uuid "521acea1-0e27-577c-b181-7478a17ba862" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326360}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- **II.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- **III.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{9}^{2}+{6}^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186198750 :question/id #uuid "e6d806a7-8383-51f7-a460-be3b003d424b" :question/math-academy-id "q-177315"} {:db/id 17592186284748 :question/id #uuid "1e67e934-1049-5a47-aaca-94c1d2a3bfc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-177118" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5a4ade3a-303a-5eec-9df3-e43d050e7127" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465651} {:answer/id #uuid "bfb5336b-989f-5a31-b653-6429b31a077f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465652}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465651} :answer-field/id #uuid "50d64a07-1676-5fda-bef0-6a4849be81d2" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466669} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6722f30e-e2af-5a70-879f-cfff27425f84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465653} {:answer/id #uuid "dc3d0a9a-fffb-56ce-a7bd-59c663e5f87e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465654}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465653} :answer-field/id #uuid "c9cb2af9-89d8-5f3d-8d83-90156885a877" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466670} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9ff5d22d-d9d1-5f3d-acef-b6be4a77c7ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465655} {:answer/id #uuid "bb044ed9-c0d7-5063-b76d-362678932554" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465656}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465655} :answer-field/id #uuid "3cba7c41-2ad1-5047-8e7d-0cc187a92400" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466671}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- **II.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- **III.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}=-\frac{12}{25}+\frac{12}{25}=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{4}{5})^{2}+(\frac{3}{5})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(-\frac{3}{5})^{2}+(\frac{4}{5})^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186284764 :question/id #uuid "e16f6fa7-ae80-51bb-bdf3-1add916dcb13" :question/math-academy-id "q-178269" :knowledge-point/_questions 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$

II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthonormal

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=6+3\ne 0.
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that, $Q({u}_{1})⊥̸Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}\ne 0.
$$

- Statement III is false since the set is not even orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186406655 :question/id #uuid "9892c6c7-24de-57f2-a3e8-0b32de0c1349" :question/math-academy-id "q-40491" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "047c19ef-c76a-57b3-b13e-81cac8438947" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186473112} {:answer/id #uuid "0f411e21-0bfc-5e60-be10-aa9385c60d56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186473113}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186473113} :answer-field/id #uuid "41b5e6b2-6fa4-5699-91d3-98491ea01274" :answer-field/key "U" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473951} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b5e99f8-6d7b-5605-8eeb-768c689a1a11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186473114} {:answer/id #uuid "d3e8b7c2-03e8-52a8-8c30-1f1597b0a406" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186473115}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186473114} :answer-field/id #uuid "2909a2f7-876c-5e10-a289-6837f83679fc" :answer-field/key "V" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473952} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "829a1b56-ccd5-5381-aeca-6ba71098f21a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186473116} {:answer/id #uuid "adcc7d05-7e81-525a-b650-a03adf317913" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186473117}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186473117} :answer-field/id #uuid "51b28bdf-55b7-5470-b1f6-bd8182431d5f" :answer-field/key "W" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473953}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following are orthogonal sets?
- **U.** $U={Q(\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$
- **W.** $W={Q(\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix})}$
- **V.** $V={Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})},\,$ ${Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})},\,$ and $\,{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})}.$ 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=1-1=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=2+12-5=9\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only"."} {:db/id 17592186411865 :question/id #uuid "8d807e12-6960-57f6-b74d-aa3fe66f0f76" :question/math-academy-id "q-178271"} {:db/id 17592186415156 :question/id #uuid "2a7fbace-2464-5d79-be05-e6f28745c3de" :question/math-academy-id "q-178014" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "81d08864-6101-5251-8351-5c0043998d07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186472778} {:answer/id #uuid "1a22dbe5-0d2b-5c0a-9531-8c54bafdc81e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186472779}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186472779} :answer-field/id #uuid "71e4259d-b2ae-5c52-927d-7cf47899f776" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473784} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c84ccb50-f1be-591e-8bac-35014caba949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186472780} {:answer/id #uuid "19621db5-93e2-50ee-9ddb-8440f2d6f313" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186472781}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186472781} :answer-field/id #uuid "7af95f9f-6948-54ed-b3d3-37b3b7e7a68c" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473785} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5b309452-f7e7-54e9-bbdf-9a3025bd85c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186472782} {:answer/id #uuid "f4968354-f03a-5157-9f0d-8be8dbd50643" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186472783}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186472782} :answer-field/id #uuid "46245871-924f-5edd-8bb1-a6c28bc755b4" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473786}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

transformation** if for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

$$
\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}.
$$

In this case, we say that $\mathbf{Q}$ *preserves the dot product*.

The linear transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is orthogonal.

- $\| \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \| = \| \mathbf{x} \|$. In other words, $\mathbf{Q}$ preserves vector norms.

- If $\mathbf{x} \perp \mathbf{y}$ then $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \perp \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y})$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$ In general, $\mathbf{Q}$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $\mathbf{Q}$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set." :tutorial/id #uuid "fed8f501-fcb5-5852-bf23-1e999e4c9e1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8098 :tutorial/title Find $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)$, where $x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}$ and $y=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

$$

$$

$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{9}^{2}+{6}^{2}}\ne 1.

:db/id 17592186446167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ac6fbe63-89e3-55f0-b383-00653c46559a" :question/math-academy-id "q-178025" :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$

II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} :step/id #uuid "024575a8-c8f0-5c99-9c1d-bf6941663ece" :step/next {:db/id 17592186446171}} {:db/id 17592186446171 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284764 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e1f6862c-27fd-5c39-8eb2-3cbbffed6df8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465669} {:answer/id #uuid "786a7ab2-a3ec-5b80-8a00-e9e1753b87d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465670}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465669} :answer-field/id #uuid "55fa8074-b199-52f0-b9ec-a64e6d2e74dd" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466678} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14cbd69a-f982-5d8b-a7b5-faa1d54ef043" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465671} {:answer/id #uuid "a3dbd501-b3c0-564f-92ea-a9a572fb9e89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465672}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465671} :answer-field/id #uuid "77082866-697e-5473-bb08-593811756def" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466679} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "270b69ea-ae43-51a2-bc71-ac5760e7b855" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465673} {:answer/id #uuid "f89e42f6-9f2a-5d60-9603-c8642f276749" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465674}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465673} :answer-field/id #uuid "07d18537-0a6d-59ae-9629-b8bdfac0f081" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466680}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e16f6fa7-ae80-51bb-bdf3-1add916dcb13" :question/math-academy-id "q-178269" :question/problem "$$

{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$

II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} :step/id #uuid "024575a8-c8f0-5c99-9c1d-bf6941663ece" :step/next {:db/id 17592186446171}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosecant function is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\arcsch x) = -\dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+x^2}}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(1-x)) \\  & =7\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(1-x)) \\  & =7(-\frac{1}{|1-x|\sqrt{1+(1-x)^{2}}})\cdot (1-x)^{′} \\  & =7(-\frac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{1+1-2x+{x}^{2}}})\cdot (-1) \\  & =\frac{7}{|x-1|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-2x+2}}.\end{aligned}

\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

In this case, the expression for $f(x)$  is a product $u(x) \cdot v(x)$ with $u(x) = \sin{x}$ and $v(x) = \arcsch{x}.$ 

Therefore, we apply the product rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{arcsch}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x)^{′} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{arcsch}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x+{{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}})}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x) = -\dfrac{\sin{x}}{|x|\sqrt{1+x^2}}.$"} {:db/id 17592186048842} {:db/id 17592186167348 :question/id #uuid "0a9c50a0-b824-574f-b6ba-748b65c80ad1" :question/math-academy-id "q-95343"} {:db/id 17592186167349 :question/id #uuid "c64b6497-cde2-5c37-b145-e4237792aec0" :question/math-academy-id "q-95345" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166768 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f5e40340-35cf-50ee-8a0d-7eb873490693" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Product and Quotient Rules"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dc066d2d-b967-54ed-b8f8-371c35e04719" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186165304} {:answer/id #uuid "023cd180-82b9-5f2f-97cc-1d0b3c92fb24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(1)/(2x(1 + x^{2}))" :db/id 17592186165305} {:answer/id #uuid "28d5698f-cc98-5192-ba19-39a588d1de5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(1)/(x^{2}(1 - x^{2}))" :db/id 17592186165306} {:answer/id #uuid "48358194-289a-5796-b113-74109d831b21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(2)/(3x(1 - x^{2}))" :db/id 17592186165307} {:answer/id #uuid "4c62934d-7dba-5030-b6d9-d9c1af75cabf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}" :db/id 17592186165308}] :answer-field/id #uuid "c55b12a9-d490-5b9e-a4aa-41e0c6ac6898" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186165303}] :question/problem "If $f(x) = \frac{arcoth x}{x^{2}}$, then $f^{′}(x) = g(x) - \frac{2arcoth x}{x^{3}}$. the inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions are shown below:
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}, &  & x\in (0,1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the derivative of the base inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions, we can differentiate combinations of these functions, by using the properties of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of

$$
y = \arsech{(-x^2)}
$$

Using the formulas above together with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡(-{x}^{2})) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-{x}^{2})\sqrt{1-{(-{x}^{2})}^{2}}}\cdot {(-{x}^{2})}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{-{x}^{2}\sqrt{1-{x}^{4}}}\cdot (-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc2da505-a8d0-5680-b8a0-ddeb66c32295" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5210 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "20757712-075c-58c5-8cc7-4422f34ec28e" :step/math-academy-id 32695 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167597}}] :activity/title "Differentiating Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186167021} {:db/id 17592186167702 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168092 :tutorial/content "The derivatives of the inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions are shown below:

The instantaneous rate of change at $x=2$ is
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4ln⁡x-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{x}+5) \\  & =\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{x}ln⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{x}ln⁡(2))|}_{x=2} \\  & =\frac{4}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{2}ln⁡(2) \\  & =2-\frac{4}{3}ln⁡(2)\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186401627 :question/id #uuid "104d7814-9b21-55a2-864d-c61ec56f5c8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-17392"} {:db/id 17592186096615 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id :question/problem "Given the function $y=2{x}^{3}+x-3{log}_{6}⁡x,$ find the instantaneous rate of change at $x=3.$ Do not round the answer.

The instantaneous rate of change at $x=3$ is
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To differentiate a logarithm with base $a,$ we use the formula

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{a}⁡x)=\frac{1}{xln⁡a}.
$$

To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}+x-3{log}_{6}⁡x) \\  & =2\cdot 3{x}^{2}+1-3\cdot \frac{1}{xln⁡6} \\  & =6{x}^{2}+1-\frac{3}{xln⁡6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=3} & ={(6{x}^{2}+1-\frac{3}{xln⁡6})|}_{x=3} \\  & =6(3)^{2}+1-\frac{3}{3\cdot ln⁡6} \\  & =55-\frac{1}{ln⁡6}\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186314913 :question/id #uuid "6065f3ff-ff9c-5643-832d-8d1ba7e4dfa6" :question/math-academy-id "q-340105"} {:db/id 17592186314914 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
		&= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( \log_4 x + \ln x \right)\
		&= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\log_4 x) + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\ln x )\
		&= \dfrac{1}{x\ln 4} + \dfrac{1}{x}.
}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{1}{xln⁡4}+\frac{1}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{ln⁡4}+1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050711} {:db/id 17592186480730} {:db/id 17592186097136 :question/id #uuid "0259cf05-81de-512b-a7bb-bd7b4b70d4e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-17373"} {:db/id 17592186097137 :question/id #uuid "55e0676e-8226-56ea-844c-41bb8f4c2189" :question/math-academy-id "q-17395"} {:db/id 17592186233052 :question/id #uuid "2ae057d0-d78b-5718-aa6f-daab4feb4650" :question/math-academy-id "q-101723"} {:db/id 17592186233902 :question/id #uuid "203042d7-3a90-5b98-a3a8-41d259d10f67" :question/math-academy-id "q-340014"} {:db/id 17592186233903 :question/id #uuid "7cc61275-8b03-5f03-bb68-53ecece9ebf0" :question/math-academy-id "q-340022"} {:db/id 17592186233905 :question/id #uuid "25397da2-818c-507a-82b9-e23dda017608" :question/math-academy-id "q-340109"} {:db/id 17592186234289 :question/id #uuid "e390b863-0cc7-5db5-bfcb-f1828e76e02e" :question/math-academy-id "q-70897"} {:db/id 17592186237854 :question/id #uuid "09ca9b0e-b19f-5aca-b14f-466e3c4366f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-101726"} {:db/id 17592186284696 :question/id #uuid "9bd05e5a-ceb5-5b6d-a1ee-24c21df80b24" :question/math-academy-id "q-17371"} {:db/id 17592186314899 :question/id #uuid "1eb887e7-89db-539c-9d35-d652e9bb15c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-340024"} {:db/id 17592186314901 :question/id #uuid "1b69d4c2-7ebc-59ed-aa14-566d23bb3592" :question/math-academy-id "q-340026"} {:db/id 17592186314915 :question/id #uuid "5c352abb-1992-52cb-94e7-b48e48f5bbc8" :question/math-academy-id "q-340110"} {:db/id 17592186403412 :question/id #uuid "ddfac57c-89c4-597b-b080-b0ac4a48d4c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-70903"} {:db/id 17592186048434} {:db/id 17592186049332 :topic/difficulty 1.1080081482350719 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428027 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( \log_a x \right)= \dfrac{1}{x\ln a}.
$$

Also, recall that whenever $\log$ is written without a base, we can assume that it represents the base $10.$ So, we have

$$
\log x =  \log_{10} x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{log}x) & =\frac{d}{dx}({log}_{10}x)=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}10}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To see where this rule comes from, we can use the change-of-base formula as shown below.

$$
\log_a x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln a}
$$

Taking the derivative and using the fact that $\ln a$ is a constant, then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{a}x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}x}{\operatorname{ln}a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}a}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}a}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}a}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7a7450e4-ec0e-5a5e-9c86-9430eb889be7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2616 :tutorial/title "Differentiating a Logarithmic Function with a General Base"} :step/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "e-6117" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186179666 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5ee41f2-7116-52f4-b1f7-923997d994ab" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition Using a Difference of Squares"}] :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- $P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[4, 6]$

- $P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[2, 6]$

Calculate  $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \Delta y_j,$ where $\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}$ and $\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j.
$$

Note that $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j$ is just the length of the interval $[2, 6].$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=6-2=4.\end{aligned}
$$

For the sum over $i,$ we can evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}({x}_{i}+{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i} & =({x}_{1}+{x}_{0})Δ{x}_{1}+({x}_{2}+{x}_{1})Δ{x}_{2}+⋯+({x}_{m}+{x}_{m-1})Δ{x}_{m} \\  & =({x}_{1}\,+\,{x}_{0})({x}_{1}\,-\,{x}_{0})+({x}_{2}\,+\,{x}_{1})({x}_{2}\,-\,{x}_{1})+({x}_{m}\,+\,{x}_{m-1})({x}_{m}\,-\,{x}_{m-1}) \\  & =({x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})+({x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{1}^{2})+⋯+({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{m-1}^{2}) \\  & =(\cancel{{x}_{1}^{2}}-{x}_{0}^{2})+(\cancel{{x}_{2}^{2}}-\cancel{{x}_{1}^{2}})+⋯+({x}_{m}^{2}-\cancel{{x}_{m-1}^{2}}) \\  & =-{x}_{0}^{2}+{x}_{m}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={6}^{2}-{4}^{2} \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we finally arrive at 

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j = 20\cdot 4 = 80.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049943} {:db/id 17592186180268 :question/id #uuid "a88af1ba-c0a1-5207-b3ae-5df258155f41" :question/math-academy-id "q-72129" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179666 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5ee41f2-7116-52f4-b1f7-923997d994ab" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition Using a Difference of Squares"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "95d34ba7-f70e-5bde-a60f-f0c96ad96341" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186179153} {:answer/id #uuid "c56bbebc-c48f-5c5c-b940-c2f97f2af460" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186179154} {:answer/id #uuid "e8802437-9f26-5e47-b836-a50a564ead55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186179155} {:answer/id #uuid "0c1ec69d-8237-53ab-b125-deba7bb578fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186179156} {:answer/id #uuid "31e69d82-7c37-5b8c-a0a6-d027fcca6a8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "48" :db/id 17592186179157}] :answer-field/id #uuid "376d3cb3-e1a1-527b-b302-47ad3abeeb22" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186179152}] :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}={{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}}$ is a partition of the interval $[3,5]$

- ${P}_{2}={{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}}$ is a partition of the interval $[-1,2]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}+{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}+{y}_{j-1})Δ{y}_{j}.
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ is just the length of the interval $[3,5].$ So, we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}=5-3=2.
$$

For the sum over $j,$ we evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}+{y}_{j-1})Δ{y}_{j} & =({y}_{1}+{y}_{0})Δ{y}_{1}+({y}_{2}+{y}_{1})Δ{y}_{2}+⋯+({y}_{n}+{x}_{n-1})Δ{y}_{n} \\  & =({y}_{1}+{y}_{0})({y}_{1}-{y}_{0})+({y}_{2}+{y}_{1})({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})+⋯+({y}_{n}+{x}_{n-1})({y}_{n}-{y}_{n-1}) \\  & =({y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{0}^{2})+({y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{1}^{2})+⋯+({y}_{n}^{2}-{y}_{n-1}^{2}) \\  & =(\cancel{{y}_{1}^{2}}-{y}_{0}^{2})+(\cancel{{y}_{2}^{2}}-\cancel{{y}_{1}^{2}})+⋯+({y}_{n}^{2}-\cancel{{y}_{n-1}^{2}}) \\  & =-{y}_{0}^{2}+{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{n}^{2}-{y}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}-(-1)^{2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we finally arrive at 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}+{y}_{j-1})Δ{y}_{j}=2\cdot 3=6.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186275219 :question/id #uuid "858f379b-ddc1-550e-98c2-99b0ab549552" :question/math-academy-id "q-149634"} {:db/id 17592186275220 :question/id #uuid "6ead2a91-4719-5999-bfe0-1edbb8b3c0b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-149635"} {:db/id 17592186179722 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179584 :question/id #uuid "e2f01953-2fb1-5ddb-83ae-5d8a73e7f7ac" :question/math-academy-id "e-9482"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f913fab-d0b5-5e9e-b292-039afe4a148c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048800} {:db/id 17592186049629}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186179979 :question/id #uuid "7cb18f0a-5793-5799-850f-ef66cbf9de18" :question/math-academy-id "q-122867"} {:db/id 17592186180267 :question/id #uuid "b8ba4a0f-f607-55a9-9beb-85f51bad2770" :question/math-academy-id "q-72128"} {:db/id 17592186256777 :question/id #uuid "ecb6ed16-6d45-5080-8683-a8fbdb3fa178" :question/math-academy-id "q-123069"} {:db/id 17592186275216 :question/id #uuid "ba5f3cf2-5db7-5ec1-b7c9-a70950beee5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-149628"} {:db/id 17592186339124 :question/id #uuid "9f73aa4c-df24-5091-bd74-35aefea94a85" :question/math-academy-id "q-72476"} {:db/id 17592186339125 :question/id #uuid "d6d7f627-89ab-505d-97fc-50a07131d61d" :question/math-academy-id "q-72479"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"} {:db/id 17592186179584 :question/id #uuid "e2f01953-2fb1-5ddb-83ae-5d8a73e7f7ac" :question/math-academy-id "e-9482" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186179722 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f913fab-d0b5-5e9e-b292-039afe4a148c" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"}] :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- $P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[-1, 2]$

- $P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[2, 3]$

Calculate $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n {3} \Delta x_i \Delta y_j,$ where $\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}$ and $\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}3Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\Delta x_i$ and $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[-1, 2]$ and $[2,3]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =2-(-1)=3, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
3 \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 1 = 9.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048800} {:db/id 17592186049629} {:db/id 17592186179979 :question/id #uuid "7cb18f0a-5793-5799-850f-ef66cbf9de18" :question/math-academy-id "q-122867" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179722 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f913fab-d0b5-5e9e-b292-039afe4a148c" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "43466d22-8b48-55a6-bf28-957026cac2ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186254244} {:answer/id #uuid "55b18526-955c-50d0-b566-01dce50dca98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186254419} {:answer/id #uuid "57c1775a-dfcb-570e-be88-c4c7df1d41a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186254442} {:answer/id #uuid "a4e273af-9b7d-518f-9227-01b071590528" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186255125} {:answer/id #uuid "b638c667-208e-545f-9953-26e2b3c9f50c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186255282}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "a4e273af-9b7d-518f-9227-01b071590528" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186255125} :answer-field/id #uuid "192e1cce-6291-501b-a0bd-b0d1f2458310" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186255963}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

Now, let's partition ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) into ![](images/37/37e17c4a2302e6352fb7186621c9c43bb5e99d43a8a0bc700c0181d36c6cc915.svg) rectangles of equal area, as shown below.

![](images/10/10c85c7b9034a7cd342c5360a13eca471b103e769415a3459e7841c3d948ee7d.png)

Note that we can describe our partition without a diagram as follows:

- The partition of the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-interval ![](images/10/10afad0ff28bd2c5b5f3450dd6a83c4c6263cf628e8f405c7ff0d06ed7249072.svg) can be expressed as ![](images/bf/bf81cbc93793a83bbd68b3de440efd7329b8979e6ad9ca76a755938ba1079955.svg) where ![](images/67/674ac6553524f5663674850d81bea00ec8c59ee651fd2f4c942e0ab0a8a5d790.svg) ![](images/44/44fabdac948e1c3466dde55f202f25d1c267c85e22f0d38d8a1deed12ce2a929.svg) ![](images/5a/5ad873e1f6b4b1ba4a7810e18f8ab571d5bd3f8aaa4d72401c7bd19721a389e3.svg) and ![](images/f0/f0b8129f0d98db64a6be3240f33cf4b91e651fa2f2329d0258beba183624a977.svg)

- The partition of the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-interval ![](images/2e/2e43b93bdeca20a22541e4b289efb7e37f3b6a391bfed32323c4e3a3c7cda162.svg) can be expressed as ![](images/c3/c38a1873b3c68a6d204981670a7360f59512b1b42ce835b795b6be24619a2a6a.svg) where ![](images/a9/a92c357a02416f0914aa679bd177f1d72f7b52e2f063371fe36d8db0b2a0ead6.svg) ![](images/7a/7afd61dbfbaad2470afc104718dd99118e9f4cbfa82a63b4d0abb0b2563179c7.svg) and ![](images/4a/4a6fda6532f4b6963586cfbcb6c3d2174940834d2ed22645497d48f0788ba384.svg)

![](images/0e/0e497b6d43e4d46d4fad71bc2b81810c972b0e306817d161ad3a2e285e6b9d6e.png)

Let $\Delta x_i$ be the difference in the $x$-values of any two successive points in $P_1 = \{x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}
$$

Similarly, let $\Delta y_j$ be the difference in the $y$-values of any two successive points in $P_2= \{y_0, y_1, y_2\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}
$$

It turns out that evaluating double sums over rectangular partitions is important in some parts of higher-level math. For example, how do we compute the sum below?

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j
$$

First, note that we can use the product rule for double summations to write this sum as a product of two separate sums:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j = \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j
$$

Now, recall that for partitions of intervals, the sum of differences in successive points is equal to the length of the interval.

- Here, the $x_i$'s partition the interval $[1,4]$ which has length $4 - 1 = 3.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^3 \Delta{x}_i = 3.$

- Similarly, the $y_j$'s partition the interval $[2,4]$ which has length $4 - 2 = 2.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^2 \Delta{y}_j = 2.$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is plenty of geometric intuition here.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i = 3$ represents the width of the rectangle, while $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 2$ represents the height.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j$ represents the area of the rectangle." :tutorial/id #uuid "3e13206a-d7f4-54d7-aa8c-37e9c0e3d26c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5798 :tutorial/title "Calculating a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"} :step/id #uuid "b2095dad-9a02-54e5-a167-0babe1804a2a" :step/math-academy-id 35548 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180463}}] :activity/title "Calculating Double Summations Over Partitions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179852} {:db/id 17592186180466 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180707 :tutorial/content "Just as we can form partitions of closed intervals of the real line, we can also partition rectangular regions in the Cartesian plane.

![](images/0e/0e497b6d43e4d46d4fad71bc2b81810c972b0e306817d161ad3a2e285e6b9d6e.png)

Let $\Delta x_i$ be the difference in the $x$-values of any two successive points in $P_1 = \{x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}
$$

Similarly, let $\Delta y_j$ be the difference in the $y$-values of any two successive points in $P_2= \{y_0, y_1, y_2\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}
$$

It turns out that evaluating double sums over rectangular partitions is important in some parts of higher-level math. For example, how do we compute the sum below?

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j
$$

First, note that we can use the product rule for double summations to write this sum as a product of two separate sums:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j = \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j
$$

Now, recall that for partitions of intervals, the sum of differences in successive points is equal to the length of the interval.

- Here, the $x_i$'s partition the interval $[1,4]$ which has length $4 - 1 = 3.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^3 \Delta{x}_i = 3.$

- Similarly, the $y_j$'s partition the interval $[2,4]$ which has length $4 - 2 = 2.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^2 \Delta{y}_j = 2.$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is plenty of geometric intuition here.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i = 3$ represents the width of the rectangle, while $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 2$ represents the height.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j$ represents the area of the rectangle." :tutorial/id #uuid "3e13206a-d7f4-54d7-aa8c-37e9c0e3d26c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5798 :tutorial/title "Calculating a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"} :step/id #uuid "b2095dad-9a02-54e5-a167-0babe1804a2a" :step/math-academy-id 35548 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180463}} {:db/id 17592186180710 :tutorial/content "We have our partition $P = P_1\times P_2,$ shown below.
