17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ defined above, select the correct options below.$\,$
$⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩=$
{{field-1}}

$\,$
The functions $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ and $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ 
{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We begin by using the half-angle identity

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)=\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)).
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)]}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\pi -(-\pi ))-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi )-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-6\pi )) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ and $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ $\text{are not orthogonal}$ with respect to the inner product."} {:db/id 17592186314939 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $F(x)={x}^{2}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{2}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\pi -(-\pi ))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4\pi ))) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186314988 :question/id #uuid "b8b54f2c-8781-54b8-a107-16250836e9fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-340648"} {:db/id 17592186314989 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $F(x)={x}^{2}-6x$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{4}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{4} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{4}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(16\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ & ={b}_{4}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩ \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)⟩} \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({x}^{2}-6x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186315082 :question/id #uuid "a5448f9e-c9df-59b5-abdc-33e558c56456" :question/math-academy-id "q-341309" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166964 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),1⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),1⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},1⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),1⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),1⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,1⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),1⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,1⟩.

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/math-academy-id 3195} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167943 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168034 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will represent a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ as an infinite sum of simple sine and cosine waves. This representation is called the **Fourier series** for $f(x)$:

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

The key idea is that we can "build" a complicated periodic graph by adding together basic waves. For example, below we have a discontinuous periodic function approximated by the first few terms of its Fourier series.

![](images/39/392a8df0fab00010e76036aa0fec2c60f25b5766b3cacc7983b7443d909866eb.png)

This gives us a powerful way to analyze periodic behavior by breaking it down into simple oscillations. Fourier series play a central role in modeling vibrations, signals, and other repeating patterns.

To work with Fourier series, we typically start with a function defined on a single base interval, such as $[-\pi,\pi),$ and then extend it to be periodic over all real numbers. This process creates what is called a **periodic extension**.

In the next slide, we will define this concept formally and look at some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "1d19e02d-99c0-5649-b7a3-bdb37c8e97e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14624 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "822d573c-a967-52e4-854c-d2b5f14b0fff" :step/math-academy-id 600573 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167955}} {:db/id 17592186167944 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166962 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166562 :question/id #uuid "5888d4ce-bc45-540b-afa0-901008abfcde" :question/math-academy-id "e-21787"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "544f5154-5213-5898-a45d-4546bc8004c8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049091} {:db/id 17592186049353} {:db/id 17592186050172}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167264} {:db/id 17592186167265} {:db/id 17592186311951} {:db/id 17592186314968} {:db/id 17592186315068} {:db/id 17592186315069} {:db/id 17592186413394} {:db/id 17592186413395}] :knowledge-point/title "Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c6f0ea8f-2008-5f49-84d9-7341157766fc" :step/math-academy-id 600574 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167945}} {:db/id 17592186167945 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168036 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can define an inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi)$ given by

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Also recall that functions $f$ and $g$ are called *orthogonal* (with respect to this inner product) if $\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=0.$

The key fact we will use throughout this lesson is that the functions

$$
1,\ \cos(x),\ \sin(x),\ \cos(2x),\ \sin(2x),\ \ldots
$$

are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined above.

More precisely, for integers $m,n\ge 1,$ we have the following orthogonality relations on $[-\pi,\pi)$:

- $\langle \cos(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ if $m\ne n,$

- $\langle \sin(mx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ if $m\ne n,$ and

- $\langle \sin(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $m,n.$

Also, the constant function $1$ is orthogonal to every sine and cosine:

- $\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,$ and

- $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $n\ge 1.$

Finally, we will also use the squared norms of these functions:

$$
\langle 1,1\rangle=2\pi,
\quad
\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\pi
\quad
\text{for all } n\ge 1.
$$

Let's see how this works in concrete examples.

**Note:** Both intervals $[-\pi,\pi)$ and $[0,2\pi)$ are considered standard in this context. We’ll use $[-\pi,\pi)$ in tutorials, but some exercises use $[0,2\pi).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9c1c7f37-624c-5c49-9ded-2b3dd3b37d7a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14639 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Orthogonal Functions"} :step/id #uuid "f80997bd-d9ed-5a35-b485-c34868575480" :step/math-academy-id 600578 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167946}} {:db/id 17592186167946 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166963 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166563 :question/id #uuid "052f11a0-2f27-5285-83af-6d8fdb729024" :question/math-academy-id "e-21788"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fadf4f64-3569-56b2-98e1-f6681892054a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049303} {:db/id 17592186049850} {:db/id 17592186050331}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167274} {:db/id 17592186167275} {:db/id 17592186314939} {:db/id 17592186314940} {:db/id 17592186314970} {:db/id 17592186314993} {:db/id 17592186314994} {:db/id 17592186314995} {:db/id 17592186314996} {:db/id 17592186315084} {:db/id 17592186397472} {:db/id 17592186413393}] :knowledge-point/title "Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines"} :step/id #uuid "b4a0ba44-f514-5920-a47f-39a8f107bb7d" :step/math-academy-id 600579 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167947}} {:db/id 17592186167947 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168035 :tutorial/content "Recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We can represent $f(x)$ by its Fourier series:

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

Our goal is to find the formulas for the coefficients $a_0, a_n,$ and $b_n.$

To do this, we'll use a powerful idea from linear algebra. We define an *inner product* for functions on the interval $[-\pi,\pi)$ as

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

With this inner product, the set of functions $\{1, \cos(nx), \sin(nx)\}$ for $n\ge 1$ is an *orthogonal set*.

This means we can think of the Fourier coefficients as *projections* of the function $f(x)$ onto each of these orthogonal "directions". The coefficients $a_0,a_n,b_n$ simply tell us "how much" of $f(x)$ lies in each of these directions.

On the next slide, we will use this idea to derive the formula for the first coefficient, $a_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "304c879d-2d08-5f1e-985b-938b67e64dfb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14628 :tutorial/title "Fourier Series Form For 2pi-Periodic Functions"} :step/id #uuid "769e9784-6852-5663-879d-f2dd13159e0a" :step/math-academy-id 600583 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167956}} {:db/id 17592186167948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166964 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166564 :question/id #uuid "d2127a8e-14bb-5574-a542-852333fe4cca" :question/math-academy-id "e-21789"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "304c015d-cbb6-5989-a102-d6f0f5f38604" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048169} {:db/id 17592186050841}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167282} {:db/id 17592186167291} {:db/id 17592186314985} {:db/id 17592186314987} {:db/id 17592186314988} {:db/id 17592186314989} {:db/id 17592186314991} {:db/id 17592186315082} {:db/id 17592186397418} {:db/id 17592186397438} {:db/id 17592186397539}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining Expressions For Fourier Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "52c506ad-0e1c-5f71-b513-284e3650dd10" :step/math-academy-id 600584 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167949}} {:db/id 17592186167949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168043 :tutorial/content "Once again, recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We represent $f$ by its Fourier series

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

To determine the coefficients, we use the inner product on $[-\pi,\pi)$:

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

We have already seen the derivation for the coefficient $a_0$ early in the lesson.

Now, we derive the formula for $a_n$ for $n\ge 1{:}$

- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\cos(nx){:}$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\cos(nx)\right\rangle.
$$

- Using linearity, we get

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle=a_n\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
a_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Finally, we derive the formula for $b_n$ for $n\ge 1{:}$

- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\sin(nx)\right\rangle.
$$

- Using linearity, we get

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle=b_n\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
b_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Putting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc7b8526-b305-5026-8e7d-5e426bbe1a15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14668 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formulas For the Fourier Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "4fc54380-13dd-5632-a907-a555a9ed5733" :step/math-academy-id 600587} {:db/id 17592186167955 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168052 :tutorial/content "Recall that a function $f(x)$ is *$p$-periodic* if $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$  

Now, if $F(x)$ is defined on an interval $x \in [a,b)$ of length $p,$ then its **$p$-periodic extension** $f$ is defined by the two properties:  

- $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [a,b).$

For example, let $F(x) = -x$ be defined on $x\in [0,2).$ Now, suppose $f(x)$ is the $2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/fe/fe66db8a73acee21bbd5f7c95d7598b448cb678408d2f47754ee4c30aefd5b14.png)

**Watch out!** We should always be aware of the difference between $F(x)$ and its extension $f(x).$ For instance, consider the function $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ defined on $x \in [0,\pi)$ and its $\pi$-periodic extension $f(x).$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/b1/b1299bb593554a930a12870d39c74aa8d23ea97027b9e9e253e8fda6b592e42a.png)

Notice that $f(x)$ is not just $2\sin(x)!$ But it would coincide with $2\sin(x)$ if we were to consider the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ from, say, $x \in [0,2\pi]$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bbf1ed42-199b-56dd-ba70-e35c3597339a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14853 :tutorial/title "Periodic Extensions"} :step/id #uuid "c98bd153-6ef6-5953-a668-095e59197be9" :step/math-academy-id 606168 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167944}} {:db/id 17592186167956 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168053 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the formula for the coefficient $a_0$ by taking the inner product of the entire Fourier series 

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

with the constant function $1.$

- **Step 1.** Start with the Fourier series and take the inner product of both sides with $1{:}$

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big),\,1\right\rangle
$$

- **Step 2.** Use the linearity of the inner product to distribute it across the sum:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle
$$

- **Step 3.** Apply the orthogonality property. For any $n\ge 1,$ we have $\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle=0$ and $\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle=0.$ This makes all the terms in the sums equal to zero:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle=\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
$$

- **Step 4.** Solve for $a_0.$ We just need to calculate $\langle 1,1\rangle=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} 1\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x=2\pi.$

$$
a_0=\dfrac{2\langle f(x),1\rangle}{\langle 1,1\rangle}
=\dfrac{2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x}{2\pi}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

We find the formulas for $a_n$ and $b_n$ (for $n\ge 1$) in a similar way.

- To find $a_n,$ we take the inner product of the Fourier series with $\cos(nx).$ By orthogonality, the only term that is not zero on the right-hand side is the one involving $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle = a_n \langle \cos(nx), \cos(nx)\rangle
$$

Since $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x = \pi,$ we can solve for $a_n{:}$

$$
a_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

- Similarly, to find $b_n,$ we take the inner product with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
b_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

**Note:** If $f$ is the $2\pi$-periodic extension of a function $F$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi),$ then we can replace $f(x)$ with $F(x)$ inside the integrals.

Now that we have the formulas for all the coefficients, let's work through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5d2770f-53de-5939-9ec7-4155aef67173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14854 :tutorial/title "The Formula For the Constant Term"} :step/id #uuid "a0bab88b-45ac-5613-b8cf-64b1eafabee1" :step/math-academy-id 606214 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167948}}] :activity/title "Introduction to Fourier Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166990} {:db/id 17592186167943 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168034 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will represent a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ as an infinite sum of simple sine and cosine waves. This representation is called the **Fourier series** for $f(x)$:

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

The key idea is that we can "build" a complicated periodic graph by adding together basic waves. For example, below we have a discontinuous periodic function approximated by the first few terms of its Fourier series.

![](images/39/392a8df0fab00010e76036aa0fec2c60f25b5766b3cacc7983b7443d909866eb.png)

This gives us a powerful way to analyze periodic behavior by breaking it down into simple oscillations. Fourier series play a central role in modeling vibrations, signals, and other repeating patterns.

To work with Fourier series, we typically start with a function defined on a single base interval, such as $[-\pi,\pi),$ and then extend it to be periodic over all real numbers. This process creates what is called a **periodic extension**.

Now, if $F(x)$ is defined on an interval $x \in [a,b)$ of length $p,$ then its **$p$-periodic extension** $f$ is defined by the two properties:  

- $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [a,b).$

For example, let $F(x) = -x$ be defined on $x\in [0,2).$ Now, suppose $f(x)$ is the $2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/fe/fe66db8a73acee21bbd5f7c95d7598b448cb678408d2f47754ee4c30aefd5b14.png)

**Watch out!** We should always be aware of the difference between $F(x)$ and its extension $f(x).$ For instance, consider the function $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ defined on $x \in [0,\pi)$ and its $\pi$-periodic extension $f(x).$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/b1/b1299bb593554a930a12870d39c74aa8d23ea97027b9e9e253e8fda6b592e42a.png)

Notice that $f(x)$ is not just $2\sin(x)!$ But it would coincide with $2\sin(x)$ if we were to consider the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ from, say, $x \in [0,2\pi]$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bbf1ed42-199b-56dd-ba70-e35c3597339a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14853 :tutorial/title "Periodic Extensions"} :step/id #uuid "c98bd153-6ef6-5953-a668-095e59197be9" :step/math-academy-id 606168 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167944}} {:db/id 17592186167944 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166962 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166562 :question/id #uuid "5888d4ce-bc45-540b-afa0-901008abfcde" :question/math-academy-id "e-21787"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "544f5154-5213-5898-a45d-4546bc8004c8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049091} {:db/id 17592186049353} {:db/id 17592186050172}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167264} {:db/id 17592186167265} {:db/id 17592186311951} {:db/id 17592186314968} {:db/id 17592186315068} {:db/id 17592186315069} {:db/id 17592186413394} {:db/id 17592186413395}] :knowledge-point/title "Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c6f0ea8f-2008-5f49-84d9-7341157766fc" :step/math-academy-id 600574 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167945}} {:db/id 17592186167945 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168036 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can define an inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi)$ given by

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Also recall that functions $f$ and $g$ are called *orthogonal* (with respect to this inner product) if $\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=0.$

The key fact we will use throughout this lesson is that the functions

$$
1,\ \cos(x),\ \sin(x),\ \cos(2x),\ \sin(2x),\ \ldots
$$

are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined above.

More precisely, for integers $m,n\ge 1,$ we have the following orthogonality relations on $[-\pi,\pi)$:

- $\langle \cos(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ if $m\ne n,$

- $\langle \sin(mx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ if $m\ne n,$ and

- $\langle \sin(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $m,n.$

Also, the constant function $1$ is orthogonal to every sine and cosine:

- $\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,$ and

- $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $n\ge 1.$

Finally, we will also use the squared norms of these functions:

$$
\langle 1,1\rangle=2\pi,
\quad
\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\pi
\quad
\text{for all } n\ge 1.
$$

Let's see how this works in concrete examples.

**Note:** Both intervals $[-\pi,\pi)$ and $[0,2\pi)$ are considered standard in this context. We’ll use $[-\pi,\pi)$ in tutorials, but some exercises use $[0,2\pi).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9c1c7f37-624c-5c49-9ded-2b3dd3b37d7a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14639 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Orthogonal Functions"} :step/id #uuid "f80997bd-d9ed-5a35-b485-c34868575480" :step/math-academy-id 600578 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167946}} {:db/id 17592186168036 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can define an inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi)$ given by

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

Our goal is to find the formulas for the coefficients $a_0, a_n,$ and $b_n.$

To do this, we'll use a powerful idea from linear algebra. We define an *inner product* for functions on the interval $[-\pi,\pi)$ as

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

With this inner product, the set of functions $\{1, \cos(nx), \sin(nx)\}$ for $n\ge 1$ is an *orthogonal set*.

This means we can think of the Fourier coefficients as *projections* of the function $f(x)$ onto each of these orthogonal "directions". The coefficients $a_0,a_n,b_n$ simply tell us "how much" of $f(x)$ lies in each of these directions.

On the next slide, we will use this idea to derive the formula for the first coefficient, $a_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "304c879d-2d08-5f1e-985b-938b67e64dfb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14628 :tutorial/title "Fourier Series Form For 2pi-Periodic Functions"} :step/id #uuid "769e9784-6852-5663-879d-f2dd13159e0a" :step/math-academy-id 600583 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167956}} {:db/id 17592186168035 :tutorial/content "Recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We can represent $f(x)$ by its Fourier series:

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

Our goal is to find the formulas for the coefficients $a_0, a_n,$ and $b_n.$

To do this, we'll use a powerful idea from linear algebra. We define an *inner product* for functions on the interval $[-\pi,\pi)$ as

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

With this inner product, the set of functions $\{1, \cos(nx), \sin(nx)\}$ for $n\ge 1$ is an *orthogonal set*.

This means we can think of the Fourier coefficients as *projections* of the function $f(x)$ onto each of these orthogonal "directions". The coefficients $a_0,a_n,b_n$ simply tell us "how much" of $f(x)$ lies in each of these directions.

On the next slide, we will use this idea to derive the formula for the first coefficient, $a_0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "304c879d-2d08-5f1e-985b-938b67e64dfb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14628 :tutorial/title "Fourier Series Form For 2pi-Periodic Functions"} {:db/id 17592186167956 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168053 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the formula for the coefficient $a_0$ by taking the inner product of the entire Fourier series 

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

with the constant function $1.$

- **Step 1.** Start with the Fourier series and take the inner product of both sides with $1{:}$

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big),\,1\right\rangle
$$

- **Step 2.** Use the linearity of the inner product to distribute it across the sum:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle
$$

- **Step 3.** Apply the orthogonality property. For any $n\ge 1,$ we have $\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle=0$ and $\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle=0.$ This makes all the terms in the sums equal to zero:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle=\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
$$

- **Step 4.** Solve for $a_0.$ We just need to calculate $\langle 1,1\rangle=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} 1\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x=2\pi.$

$$
a_0=\dfrac{2\langle f(x),1\rangle}{\langle 1,1\rangle}
=\dfrac{2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x}{2\pi}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

We find the formulas for $a_n$ and $b_n$ (for $n\ge 1$) in a similar way.

- To find $a_n,$ we take the inner product of the Fourier series with $\cos(nx).$ By orthogonality, the only term that is not zero on the right-hand side is the one involving $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle = a_n \langle \cos(nx), \cos(nx)\rangle
$$

Since $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x = \pi,$ we can solve for $a_n{:}$

$$
a_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

- Similarly, to find $b_n,$ we take the inner product with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
b_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

**Note:** If $f$ is the $2\pi$-periodic extension of a function $F$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi),$ then we can replace $f(x)$ with $F(x)$ inside the integrals.

Now that we have the formulas for all the coefficients, let's work through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5d2770f-53de-5939-9ec7-4155aef67173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14854 :tutorial/title "The Formula For the Constant Term"} :step/id #uuid "a0bab88b-45ac-5613-b8cf-64b1eafabee1" :step/math-academy-id 606214 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167948}} {:db/id 17592186167948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166964 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166564 :question/id #uuid "d2127a8e-14bb-5574-a542-852333fe4cca" :question/math-academy-id "e-21789"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "304c015d-cbb6-5989-a102-d6f0f5f38604" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048169} {:db/id 17592186050841}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167282} {:db/id 17592186167291} {:db/id 17592186314985} {:db/id 17592186314987} {:db/id 17592186314988} {:db/id 17592186314989} {:db/id 17592186314991} {:db/id 17592186315082} {:db/id 17592186397418} {:db/id 17592186397438} {:db/id 17592186397539}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining Expressions For Fourier Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "52c506ad-0e1c-5f71-b513-284e3650dd10" :step/math-academy-id 600584 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167949}} {:db/id 17592186167949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168043 :tutorial/content "Once again, recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We represent $f$ by its Fourier series

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).
$$

To determine the coefficients, we use the inner product on $[-\pi,\pi)$:

$$
\langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

We have already seen the derivation for the coefficient $a_0$ early in the lesson.

Now, we derive the formula for $a_n$ for $n\ge 1{:}$

- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\cos(nx){:}$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\cos(nx)\right\rangle.
$$

- Using linearity, we get

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle=a_n\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
a_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Finally, we derive the formula for $b_n$ for $n\ge 1{:}$

- First, we take the inner product of both sides with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\sin(nx)\right\rangle.
$$

- Using linearity, we get

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle=b_n\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
b_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Putting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc7b8526-b305-5026-8e7d-5e426bbe1a15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14668 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formulas For the Fourier Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "4fc54380-13dd-5632-a907-a555a9ed5733" :step/math-academy-id 600587} {:db/id 17592186168043 :tutorial/content "Once again, recall that we are considering a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous on $[-\pi,\pi).$ We represent $f$ by its Fourier series

- By orthogonality, $\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0,$ $\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ for all $k,$ and $\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0$ whenever $k\ne n,$ so

$$
\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle=b_n\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle.
$$

Since $\displaystyle \langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,$ we obtain

$$
b_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Putting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc7b8526-b305-5026-8e7d-5e426bbe1a15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14668 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formulas For the Fourier Coefficients"} {:db/id 17592186168052 :tutorial/content "Recall that a function $f(x)$ is *$p$-periodic* if $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$  

Now, if $F(x)$ is defined on an interval $x \in [a,b)$ of length $p,$ then its **$p$-periodic extension** $f$ is defined by the two properties:  

- $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [a,b).$

For example, let $F(x) = -x$ be defined on $x\in [0,2).$ Now, suppose $f(x)$ is the $2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/fe/fe66db8a73acee21bbd5f7c95d7598b448cb678408d2f47754ee4c30aefd5b14.png)

**Watch out!** We should always be aware of the difference between $F(x)$ and its extension $f(x).$ For instance, consider the function $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ defined on $x \in [0,\pi)$ and its $\pi$-periodic extension $f(x).$ The graphs of $y=F(x)$ and $y=f(x)$ are shown below.

![](images/b1/b1299bb593554a930a12870d39c74aa8d23ea97027b9e9e253e8fda6b592e42a.png)

Notice that $f(x)$ is not just $2\sin(x)!$ But it would coincide with $2\sin(x)$ if we were to consider the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)=2\sin(x)$ from, say, $x \in [0,2\pi]$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bbf1ed42-199b-56dd-ba70-e35c3597339a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14853 :tutorial/title "Periodic Extensions"} {:db/id 17592186168053 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the formula for the coefficient $a_0$ by taking the inner product of the entire Fourier series 

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)
$$

with the constant function $1.$

- **Step 1.** Start with the Fourier series and take the inner product of both sides with $1{:}$

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big),\,1\right\rangle
$$

- **Step 2.** Use the linearity of the inner product to distribute it across the sum:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle
$$

- **Step 3.** Apply the orthogonality property. For any $n\ge 1,$ we have $\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle=0$ and $\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle=0.$ This makes all the terms in the sums equal to zero:

$$
\langle f(x),1\rangle=\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
$$

- **Step 4.** Solve for $a_0.$ We just need to calculate $\langle 1,1\rangle=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} 1\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x=2\pi.$

$$
a_0=\dfrac{2\langle f(x),1\rangle}{\langle 1,1\rangle}
=\dfrac{2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x}{2\pi}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

We find the formulas for $a_n$ and $b_n$ (for $n\ge 1$) in a similar way.

- To find $a_n,$ we take the inner product of the Fourier series with $\cos(nx).$ By orthogonality, the only term that is not zero on the right-hand side is the one involving $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.$

$$
\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle = a_n \langle \cos(nx), \cos(nx)\rangle
$$

Since $\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x = \pi,$ we can solve for $a_n{:}$

$$
a_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

- Similarly, to find $b_n,$ we take the inner product with $\sin(nx){:}$

$$
b_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

**Note:** If $f$ is the $2\pi$-periodic extension of a function $F$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi),$ then we can replace $f(x)$ with $F(x)$ inside the integrals.

Now that we have the formulas for all the coefficients, let's work through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5d2770f-53de-5939-9ec7-4155aef67173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14854 :question/worked-solution "Both the first and the third logarithmic terms have a base of ${\color{blue}4}$ and an argument of ${\color{red}9}$. Therefore, we can combine them by adding their coefficients:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\log_{4} (9) - 3\log_{3} (9) + 5\log_{4} (9) &= (2 + 5)\log_{4} (9) - 3\log_{3} (9) \\
&= 7\log_{4} (9) - 3\log_{3} (9)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186115579 :question/id #uuid "f61a606a-c26c-5aed-ae99-d6209b7adc25" :question/math-academy-id "q-25691"} {:db/id 17592186115931 :question/id #uuid "9736ff00-dee9-5915-9d62-ea3fd9c4489a" :question/math-academy-id "q-66642"} {:db/id 17592186115198 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115027 :question/id #uuid "c45b5963-9e06-558c-b125-f8202e42b1af" :question/math-academy-id "e-4007"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b3a510a1-0659-5929-afc5-4554b9f8ba03" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115550 :question/id #uuid "26bf910d-6cac-5a42-bdd0-a28644ea1ce8" :question/math-academy-id "q-24169"} {:db/id 17592186115583 :question/id #uuid "48aebbef-0cfd-5d5d-a2e9-9acb1aff3ca3" :question/math-academy-id "q-25712"}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Logarithmic Expressions Containing Variable Expressions"} {:db/id 17592186115027 :question/id #uuid "c45b5963-9e06-558c-b125-f8202e42b1af" :question/math-academy-id "e-4007" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186115198 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b3a510a1-0659-5929-afc5-4554b9f8ba03" :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Logarithmic Expressions Containing Variable Expressions"}] :question/problem "Simplify $9\log_6(2x)-2\log_4(2x)-3\log_4(2x)$." :question/worked-solution "Both the second and the third logarithmic terms have a base of ${\color{blue}4}$ and an argument of ${\color{red}2x}$. "$\int 4{cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

 

Letting $\theta =2x,$ we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡2x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{cos}^{2}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =\int 4\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =2\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =2(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+x)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186250304 :question/id #uuid "c6cefcd4-0ca3-54cc-a93f-201d1a8af19f" :question/math-academy-id "q-114696"} {:db/id 17592186250305 :question/id #uuid Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /16}({cos}^{2}⁡(4x)-{sin}^{2}⁡(4x))\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =4x,$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)={cos}^{2}⁡(4x)-{sin}^{2}⁡(4x).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /16}({cos}^{2}⁡(4x)-{sin}^{2}⁡(4x))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /16} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\cdot \frac{\pi }{16})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436668 :question/id #uuid "63aa6d59-1b3d-5a26-a1f9-94507bee325e" :question/math-academy-id "q-10558"} {:db/id 17592186049084} {:db/id 17592186049612} {:db/id 17592186049810} 17592186097508 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097922 :tutorial/content "How can we calculate $\displaystyle{\int} \sin x \cos x \, \textrm{d}x?$  

Notice that we have the product of sine and cosine with the same argument $(x).$ In such cases, we can use the double-angle formula for sine to solve the integral.

Let's recall the double-angle formula for sine, which is

$$
\sin {2x}=2\sin x \cos x.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\sin x \cos x =  \dfrac{1}{2} \sin {2x}.
$$

Plugging this into our integral, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \sin x \cos x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {2x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {2x}\right )+C \[5pt]
								&=-\dfrac{1}{4} \cos {2x}+C.	
	}
$$

In general, we can use the double-angle formula for sine to solve any integral that's of the form 

$$
\int \sin\left(ax+b\right)\cos(ax+b)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

$$
y = \ln (2x+1).
$$

First notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = \ln u, \qquad u = 2x+1.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}u)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=2x+1,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "054d5bfc-280f-5da5-9576-4b4cd8668e78" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1272 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e409fa6f-b896-5f75-a481-3ece75fb28d5" :step/math-academy-id 17592186093370 :tutorial/content "The chain rule can be used to differentiate logarithmic functions like 

$$
y = \ln (2x+1).
$$

First notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = \ln u, \qquad u = 2x+1.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}u)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=2x+1,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "054d5bfc-280f-5da5-9576-4b4cd8668e78" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1272 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e409fa6f-b896-5f75-a481-3ece75fb28d5" :step/math-academy-id 2500 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093123}} {:db/id 17592186093370 :tutorial/content "The chain rule can be used to differentiate logarithmic functions like

17592186134893 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135147 :tutorial/content "As we mentioned earlier, rigid motions are **distance-preserving**.

For example, if a rigid motion maps $\triangle ABC$ to $\triangle A'B'C'$, then the corresponding sides of the triangles must be congruent:

$$
AB = A'B', \qquad AC = A'C', \qquad BC = B'C'
$$

In addition, rigid motions are **angle-preserving**, which means that the corresponding angles of the triangles must be congruent as well:

$$
m\angle A = m\angle A', \qquad m\angle B = m\angle B', \qquad m\angle C = m\angle C'
$$

Since all of the corresponding sides and angles are congruent, the triangles are congruent, and we write

$$
\triangle ABC \cong \triangle A'B'C'
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4514dc0f-bb78-52d9-a728-8a09f7cbf667" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6157 :tutorial/title "Further Properties of Rigid Motions"} :step/id #uuid "6caa4091-01f6-57a9-8303-9c7ac2687088" :step/math-academy-id 37342 :step/next {:db/id 17592186135007}} {:db/id 17592186134894 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135148 :tutorial/content "So, remember, there are *only three* types of rigid motions:

- Translations
- Rotations
- Reflections

There are two properties of rigid motions we need to know:

- *A rigid motion maps every polygon to a congruent polygon.*
- *For any pair of congruent polygons, there exists a rigid motion that maps one polygon onto another.*

Consider the diagram below. Let's use the concept of rigid motions to explain why $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ are congruent.

![](images/04/0487c9bb2a640a44e9ee67830937db4272c97f4a5f5101e43e3dcf3edd6c3a1c.png)

Notice that $\mathcal{Q}$ is the image of $\mathcal{P}$ under the action of reflection in the $x$-axis.

![](images/18/183b182e26df36c6cfe6a9d682e0f3b000bff40ce7d405255a0abfee8529a946.png)

Since $\mathcal P$ is mapped to $\mathcal Q$ under a rigid motion (reflection), $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ must be congruent." :tutorial/id #uuid "511ff35e-2666-5989-ad2f-e3e9fe541c7c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6163 :tutorial/title "Properties of Rigid Motions"} :step/id #uuid "1b767960-73f6-5f1a-86d5-06e3a151b4d8" :step/math-academy-id 37367 :step/next {:db/id 17592186135008}} {:db/id 17592186135006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135021 :tutorial/content "A **rigid motion** is any transformation that does not change the distances and angles between points. Rigid motions are also called **isometries**.

There are *only three* types of rigid motions:

- Translations
- Rotations
- Reflections

**Watch out!** The following types of transformations are *not* rigid motions:

- Dilations
- Stretches" :tutorial/id #uuid "9208af14-0cfd-5ca9-989f-3bf18330cf12" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2294 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "66e47972-9ac9-5e15-abc6-6b2f033b161a" $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4514dc0f-bb78-52d9-a728-8a09f7cbf667" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6157 :tutorial/title "Further Properties of Rigid Motions"} :step/id #uuid "6caa4091-01f6-57a9-8303-9c7ac2687088" :step/math-academy-id 37342 :step/next {:db/id 17592186135007}} {:db/id 17592186135147 :tutorial/content "As we mentioned earlier, rigid motions are **distance-preserving**.

For example, if a rigid motion maps $\triangle ABC$ to $\triangle A'B'C'$, then the corresponding sides of the triangles must be congruent:

$$
AB = A'B', \qquad AC = A'C', \qquad BC = B'C'
$$

In addition, rigid motions are **angle-preserving**, which means that the corresponding angles of the triangles must be congruent as well:

$$
m\angle A = m\angle A', \qquad m\angle B = m\angle B', \qquad m\angle C = m\angle C'
$$

Since all of the corresponding sides and angles are congruent, the triangles are congruent, and we write

$$
\triangle ABC \cong \triangle A'B'C'
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4514dc0f-bb78-52d9-a728-8a09f7cbf667" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6157 :tutorial/title "Further Properties of Rigid Motions"} {:db/id 17592186135007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133976 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133546 :question/id #uuid "25f331e5-db8f-58bd-a4a6-24d7ed09db10" :question/math-academy-id "e-2906"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "811ba45c-7467-5cef-9fb8-a8282891b607" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134180} {:db/id 17592186134469}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Rigid Motions"} :step/id #uuid "43999184-e956-5a86-8726-8697e9473d18" :step/math-academy-id 9556} {:db/id 17592186134894 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135148 :tutorial/content "So, remember, there are *only three* types of rigid motions:

$\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{3 \mid x \mid \sqrt{x^2+1}}\,\textrm d x=$" :question/worked-solution "$$
\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosecant function is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\arcsch x) = -\dfrac{1}{\mid x \mid \sqrt{1+ x^2}}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\frac{1}{3\begin{vmatrix}x & \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}}dx =-\frac{1}{3}\int - \frac{1}{\mid x\end{vmatrix}\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}dx =-\frac{1}{3}arcsch x + C
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167350 :question/id #uuid "391d90c1-4dfa-5f95-b579-f610d1d49415" :question/math-academy-id "q-95355"} {:db/id 17592186167405 :question/id #uuid "c5e0187a-01ec-5234-b328-8df7e287beca" :question/math-academy-id "q-95761"} {:db/id 17592186166770 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166608 :question/id #uuid "b72eee89-1abb-5081-b89e-6cc8735b7f54" :question/math-academy-id "e-8376"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6071303-6be5-5636-a675-66d33864a7c9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167351 :question/id #uuid "d14c432c-950c-5c71-8e55-10bda554e2e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-95356"} {:db/id 17592186167406 :question/id #uuid "fef2d4a0-63bd-50d5-be34-68f559ae65d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-95819"}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrating Using Arsech"} {:db/id 17592186166608 :question/id #uuid "b72eee89-1abb-5081-b89e-6cc8735b7f54" :question/math-academy-id "e-8376" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166770 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6071303-6be5-5636-a675-66d33864a7c9" :knowledge-point/title "Integrating Using Arsech"}] :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$\displaystyle \int \dfrac{3}{x\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,\textrm d x=$" :question/worked-solution "$$
\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic secant function is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\arsech x) = -\dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{1-x^2}}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\frac{3}{x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dx =-3\int - \frac{1}{x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dx =-3arsech x + C
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167351 :question/id #uuid "d14c432c-950c-5c71-8e55-10bda554e2e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-95356"} {:db/id 17592186167406 :question/id #uuid "fef2d4a0-63bd-50d5-be34-68f559ae65d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-95819" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166770 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6071303-6be5-5636-a675-66d33864a7c9" :knowledge-point/title "Integrating Using Arsech"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "92e359c5-fca2-5e90-a057-0183a022316d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}arsech x + C" :db/id 17592186165645} {:answer/id #uuid "a7860c37-9b5f-5e52-afd2-579d9065f5e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}arcsch x + C" :db/id 17592186165646} {:answer/id #uuid "dfc5e41e-95d8-5123-bee0-7be6f32cdcd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\sqrt{2}arsech x + C" :db/id 17592186165647} {:answer/id #uuid "22916384-aa4c-5505-8483-f114834f2fe2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}arsech x + C" :db/id 17592186165648} {:answer/id #uuid "4e6fef5e-dc58-50d6-9f1a-5f48c428f6c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}arsech x + C" :db/id 17592186165649}] :answer-field/id #uuid "8f01b2e8-db8e-5abb-b7a2-af954c49c8a7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186165644}] :question/problem "What is $\displaystyle \int(1)/(x\sqrt{2(1 - "b08bfe8b-9e44-5137-a3d9-56d3138b6315" :step/math-academy-id 31217 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167712}} {:db/id 17592186167704 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168094 :tutorial/content "Recall the following derivatives of the inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{d}{dx}(arcsch x) &= -\frac{1}{\mid x \mid \sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}, & x ∈ (- ∞, 0)∪(0, ∞) \\ \frac{d}{dx}(arsech x)|=-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}, & x ∈ (0, 1) \\ \frac{d}{dx}(arcoth x)|= \frac{1}{1 - x^{2}}, & x ∈ (- ∞,-1)∪(1, ∞)\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we arrive at the following basic integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}\int\frac{1}{\mid x \mid \sqrt{1 + x^{2}}}dx &= -arcsch x + C, & x ∈ (- ∞, 0)∪(0, ∞) \\ \int\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dx|=-arsech x + C, & x ∈ (0, 1) \\ \int\frac{1}{1 - x^{2}}dx|= arcoth x + C, & x ∈ (- ∞,-1)∪(1, ∞)\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now use these formulas for finding integrals. For example, let's find the integral

$$
\int \left(\dfrac{2}{3x\sqrt{1-x^2}} + \cos x \right) \textrm d x
$$

Using the properties of integration and the formulas above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int(\frac{2}{3x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} + \cos x)dx &= \frac{2}{3}\int\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}dx + \int\cos xdx \\
&=-\frac{2}{3}arsech x + \sin x + C
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "77d4740c-3cac-5695-aa67-597e3c0ce164" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5213 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "36d709c0-168f-57e9-9ba0-9651411edeb8" :step/math-academy-id 32698 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167601}} {:db/id 17592186167712 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168102 :tutorial/content "Recall that

$$
\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = {\color{blue}\artanh{x}} + C, \qquad {\color{blue}x\in(-1,1)}
$$

But we have just seen that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = {\color{red}\arcoth{x}} + C, \qquad {\color{red}x\in(-\infty,-1) \cup (1,\infty)}
$$

Notice that the integral on the left-hand side is the same but we used different functions on the right. What is the difference, and how do we know which hyperbolic function to use?

The difference is the domain of the variable $x$. When the $\mid x \mid < 1$, we use the antiderivative $\artanh{x}$, otherwise we use the antiderivative $\arcoth{x}$.

For instance, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{1 - x^{2}}dx &= \left.artanh x\right|_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\
&= artanh (\frac{1}{2}) - artanh (-\frac{1}{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that since the limits of integration lie in the interval $(-1,1)$, we used the antiderivative $\artanh{x}$.

While, on the other hand, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{1 - x^{2}}dx &= \left.arcoth x\right|_{2}^{3} \\
&= arcoth (3) - arcoth (2)
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that since the limits of integration lie in the interval $(1,\infty)$, we used the antiderivative $\arcoth{x}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "169c2d19-f0a1-557e-88ed-519503440186" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5227 :tutorial/title "The Importance of the Domain When Integrating Using Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions"} :step/id #uuid "6157bd21-aca9-574c-a8ba-03e7aad7c93f" :step/math-academy-id 32720}] :activity/title "Integration Using Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186167022} {:db/id 17592186167704 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168094 :tutorial/content "Recall the following derivatives of the inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-6I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162042 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161836 :question/id #uuid "bba077a6-56c6-5137-b949-26fae1c98625" :question/math-academy-id "e-8633"} :knowledge-point/id - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{10} \\ 2\sqrt{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186370697 :question/id #uuid "f5a19d61-895b-51bb-abe5-e33bbbd340f5" :question/math-academy-id "q-363836"} {:db/id 17592186381942 :question/id #uuid $$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423863 :question/id #uuid "bd607d3f-88f1-5057-a261-73a39b9023d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-363834"} {:db/id 17592186430360 :question/id #uuid {{field-3}}.

|  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |

that we can rewrite as

</table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186443408 :question/id #uuid "dd93c01d-3a4b-5e26-802f-bf34131bc696" :question/math-academy-id "q-363664" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid </table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{2}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & 0 & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162043 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161837 :question/id #uuid "4fd6d412-d080-5fd1-9318-65a0f5f02dc6" :question/math-academy-id "e-8634"} :knowledge-point/id {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162725 :question/id #uuid "dcd0e8b8-71e5-5dcd-a370-0847d15e9434" :question/math-academy-id "q-98797" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162043 :knowledge-point/id #uuid
